qtut4t.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / DevSecOps The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added two security flaws impacting Cisco and GitLab software to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score: 10.0) - An integer overflow or wraparound vulnerability in GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition that could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration due to insufficient regular expression validation. CVE-2026-76418 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An unchecked return value to NULL pointer dereference vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. The development comes after Cisco said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability earlier this month. It has not publicly identified the attackers, the number of targeted organizations, or the actions taken by attackers after gaining initial access. As for CVE-2026-97229, its addition relates to a security incident disclosed by Alpine Linux in which an unknown threat actor unsuccessfully attempted to exploit the flaw targeting its instance on October 20 and 21, 2026. Specifically, the attacker probed an unpatched GitLab instance by sending crafted CI configurations, causing the GitLab worker processes to crash eight times. In four of those crashes, the exploit failed at the next step. The threat actor also downloaded Alpine Linux's GitLab container image. Subsequent attempts by the attacker to get back in on October 25 and 26 were blocked. "The attack came close to working," the maintainers of the security-focused Linux distribution said. "We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with." In light of active exploitation, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 1, 2026.

xhqa1i.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Cyber Attack / Cryptocurrency Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that a "security incident" on its platform has impacted about $6.3 billion worth of assets. The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said nearly $3 billion of those assets have been frozen on-chain so far. Tether and Circle said they have frozen more than 1.567 billion USDT and 800 million USDT related to the incident, respectively. The Arbitrum Security Council is said to have executed a transaction to freeze about $30.5 million from the Binance Exploit. "Initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," Binance said in an update. The company said there is no evidence of a wallet private key leak, adding it will cover all losses from the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) fund and its own funds. Out of an abundance of caution, Binance has also taken the following steps - Temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed Revoked the affected address authorization; Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds "We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice," Binance said. In an update, Binance said it expects withdrawals to resume in 48 hours, after its team "completes a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses." The development makes it the biggest cryptocurrency heist recorded to date, surpassing the theft of about $1.5 billion from Bybit in February 2025. The incident was subsequently attributed to North Korea. "Our current estimate on the amount stolen is approximately $5.912 billion at time of theft, nearly 4x the amount stolen in the next largest crypto heist," blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis said in an X post. Attributed to North Korea's TraderTraitor TRM Labs has attributed the record-breaking hack targeting Binance to threat actors from North Korea with high confidence. The blockchain analytics company attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which was also behind the 2025 Bybit heist. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," TRM Labs said. "The laundering observed so far, built on large swaps through market makers and lending protocols, differs from the bridge-heavy pattern that followed Bybit." TRM Labs said preparation for the attack was underway at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers taking over a Binance hot wallet to send its "entire balance to an attacker-controlled address" - At 20:20 UTC, the operator submitted a single transaction containing 50 authorizations. Each was signed by the Binance hot wallet, and each pointed it to a sweeper contract that accepts instructions only from the operator. Every wallet keeps a running count of its transactions, called a nonce, and an authorization works only at the count the wallet has reached at the moment it executes. The Binance hot wallet processes a steady flow of withdrawals, so its count keeps moving forward. By preparing signatures for 50 consecutive counts, the attacker guaranteed that one would still be valid when the transaction executed. One matched, which was all the attacker needed. The signatures were produced in advance as a batch. Three minutes and 24 seconds after the delegation, the operator instructed the Binance hot wallet to send its entire balance to an attacker-controlled address. That single transaction moved 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens, including 1.615 billion USDT. The most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance's hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains. The batch of 50 pre-signed authorizations suggests the access may have been limited in time, or that signatures had to be requested through a system. Binance has yet to publish a root cause. So far, Tether, Circle, Ripple, and World Liberty Financial have frozen about $2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council has frozen about $30 million in ETH and ARB. The attacker continues to retain control of more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, worth about $2.4 billion, plus smaller amounts on other chains.

fu3q9x.text: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance is investigating a potential security breach involving up to $5.8 billion in digital assets, in what could become the largest cryptocurrency hack in history. If confirmed stolen, the amount would far exceed the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit by North Korean hackers in February 2025, the largest confirmed crypto heist on record. The suspected breach has already prompted stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle to freeze more than $2.3 billion in assets associated with the incident. In a statement to BleepingComputer, a Binance spokesperson confirmed that the exchange was investigating reports of a potential security issue while reassuring customers that their funds were safe. "Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating. Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," the spokesperson told BleepingComputer. "Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information." Binance also warned customers to remain cautious of scams and avoid unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao (CZ) said on X that the incident appeared to be a hack, while noting that he no longer manages the exchange and expects all user funds to be fully covered. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company had frozen more than $1.567 billion in USDT associated with the potential Binance hack. Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire also confirmed that the company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC linked to the incident, adding that Circle was coordinating with law enforcement and would continue supporting the investigation. Billions transferred from Binance hot wallets The statements follow reports of billions of dollars in cryptocurrency being transferred from multiple Binance hot wallets to a newly created Ethereum address. According to blockchain transaction analysis shared on X by crypto journalist StarPlatinum, a Binance hot wallet known as "Binance 14" transferred approximately $2.53 billion across 64 cryptocurrency tokens, followed 24 seconds later by another $174.4 million from a second Binance wallet. A later update claimed that a third Binance hot wallet transferred another 780 million USDC to the same Ethereum address, bringing the reported total to approximately $3.48 billion. Meanwhile, blockchain intelligence platform Arkham Intelligence is tracking 55 cryptocurrency addresses under an entity labeled "binance-hacker-1029," with combined holdings valued at approximately $5.78 billion. The tracked assets include approximately $1.77 billion in USDT, $1.44 billion in Bitcoin, $876 million in Ethereum, and $823 million in USDC. Blockchain explorer Etherscan has also labeled the initial receiving address as "Binance Hot Wallet Exploiter 2," assigning it both "Exploit" and "Heist" tags. Etherscan labels suspected Binance exploiter wallet holding $2.27 billion. Source: BleepingComputer However, it should be noted that Arkham's $5.78 billion figure is the value of assets held across all tracked wallets, rather than a confirmed amount stolen from Binance. Binance has not yet confirmed whether the transfers were unauthorized, how the suspected breach occurred, or the total value of any stolen assets. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available. 1g1hkgy.text: A cryptomining and backdoor campaign that abuses Hugging Face model repositories came back within days of being taken down. Its most popular malicious model was downloaded more than 28,000 times. Separately, researchers flagged a fake Solana starter kit on GitHub, live since late 2025, that is positioned to trick AI coding agents into installing a remote access trojan. Code runs before the model loads Researchers at Pluto Security found 31 malicious repositories across seven Hugging Face accounts, published in two waves since September. The models pose as small Qwen2 test checkpoints. They target GPU hosts running self-hosted inference servers such as Xinference and GPUStack. With linked models included, the repositories have more than 32,000 downloads. Pluto notes that this counts downloads, not confirmed infections. Instead of using poisoned weights or pickle exploits, the campaign abuses a Hugging Face option, trust_remote_code, that lets a model ship its own Python code. When a user enables it, that code runs on their machine as soon as the model loads. The most downloaded model, MENXIANGYU/qwen2-tiny, contained no actual model at all. Its code quietly installs a cryptocurrency miner disguised as a Linux system process, restarts it if killed, and removes competing miners from the machine. Some versions also open a reverse shell, giving the attacker direct access to the infected server. Back within days of takedown Pluto found the campaign through a test account whose leftover backup files pointed to the attacker's main accounts. It reported the first wave to Hugging Face and China's ModelScope, and both removed the accounts. How Pluto linked the test account to the campaign's main accounts (Pluto Security) A second wave of 19 repositories appeared under new accounts within days. Hours after Pluto reported it, the operator published another model with a script that can break out of a container and take over the server underneath. Pluto says the second-wave repositories were still live eight days after it reported them. Downloads of the flagship model climbed from 7,354 at the time of the report to 28,412 by October 28. As of writing, Hugging Face has disabled access to that model. A near-identical copy uploaded on October 25 by a newer account, htt0118, is still live, and BleepingComputer confirmed it contains the same miner and reverse shell: 'htt0118/qwen2-tiny' model still live on Hugging Face at the time of writing (BleepingComputer) Clean scans, real payouts Hugging Face scans uploads with antivirus and partner tools from Protect AI and JFrog. Pluto says these look for known malware and unsafe model formats, rather than what a model's Python code actually does. "The second-wave flagship scanned clean while it collected 28,412 downloads," the researchers said, adding that JFrog reported the payload file was "not a machine-learning model." According to Pluto, the operator's main wallet has received roughly $5,000 in Pearl (PRL) cryptocurrency. It was still active on mining pools after the repositories behind it were removed. While the researchers watched, nine machines that appear to belong to a shared research GPU cluster started mining for the operator at once. They dropped off about six minutes later, which Pluto says fits an admin killing the jobs. Pluto attributes the campaign to a financially motivated, Chinese-speaking operator. It cites Simplified Chinese code comments, command-and-control servers on Alibaba Cloud, and activity times that fall late at night in China. Anyone who loaded these models with trust_remote_code enabled should treat the machine as compromised, check it against the indicators in Pluto's report, and rotate any credentials it could reach. Killing the miner alone doesn't remove the backdoors. Fake Solana kit targets AI coding agents In a separate report, Air Security describes a GitHub repository, SolanaUpdateTools/solana-starter-kit, that it says ranks as the top result when AI coding agents search for a Solana starter kit. An agent that picks the repository and follows its README could run the attacker's command without the developer ever seeing it. The repository was created in November 2025 and has 286 stars. Its README promises a full Solana app template, but none of that code exists, and the README is the only file in the repository: Fake Solana starter kit still live on GitHub at the time of writing (BleepingComputer) The README's only "installation" step tells users to paste a PowerShell one-liner into a command prompt. The Windows-only command assembles a URL on developer-update[.]app from fragments, then fetches and runs a script from it in memory. BleepingComputer obtained the archived payload from the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine and confirmed Air's findings. The payload installs NetSupport Manager, a legitimate remote-access tool, configured to connect to maxwintodaybtc[.]com and give the attacker hidden control of the machine at every login. The script then displays a fake error saying "developer functionality is temporarily paused due to load" and to "try again in 72 hours," which an agent could easily relay as a routine server hiccup. Fake error message displayed by the PowerShell payload (BleepingComputer) Air linked the setup to a known NetSupport RAT operator tracked by eSentire, and to an earlier campaign that lured crypto traders with fake TradingView "AI signal" tools. The payload URL returned a 404 when Air checked. At the time of writing, the GitHub repository was still live. v7vf4l.text: Japan Airlines (JAL) has announced that a data breach at Amadeus’s Passenger Service System exposed the data of about 92,000 customers. JAL Group, which operates the airlines JAL and Japan Transocean Air, uses the system to handle passenger reservations, ticketing, and check-in. According to its announcement, Amadeus notified the airline on October 23, 2026, that unauthorized access to its systems occurred between August 10, 2023, and September 23, 2026. As a result of this lengthy breach, the threat actor accessed reservation codes (PNRs), names, flight dates, routes, and travel classes for approximately 90,000 customers. An additional 2,000 customers had the above data types exposed, plus their email addresses, phone numbers, passport numbers, nationalities, frequent flyer numbers, and flight, ticket, and seat numbers. JAL says credit card numbers and passwords were not compromised, and assured that it currently has no evidence of customer information being misused. The company said Amadeus has now implemented the necessary security measures and flight operations are unaffected. Broader impact Amadeus is an IT firm that provides solutions for travel agencies, airlines, airports, and hotels. It is a major tech supplier to global aviation, used by over four hundred airlines, 210 airport operators, 34 cruise and ferry lines, and 2 million hotels. Amadeus published a statement on its website on October 1, 2026, announcing it had discovered a vulnerability in its travel booking display environment that could expose travelers’ data. At the time, the company said ransomware actors had not exploited the flaw and assured that no payment or other financial data had been exposed. As JAL has confirmed now, the vulnerability appears to have been maliciously exploited. It appears they were not the only victim of the campaign. All Nippon Airways (ANA) has also announced a customer data breach earlier today tied to Amadeus, according to local media. The airline has also suspended certain related services on its website and mobile app since October 21, although that action appears linked to the PHP2Shell threat rather than the Amadeus incident. Other airlines that have confirmed impact from the Amadeus flaw are Asiana Airlines and Korean Air, both major South Korean carriers. BleepingComputer has asked Amadeus for more information about the scope of the impact, specifically whether more airlines and other countries/markets were affected, but the company has not provided more information as of publication. 130omu0.text: Prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily suspended trading on Thursday after hackers compromised a third-party service to distribute cryptocurrency-draining JavaScript, with approximately $2.5 million in assets traced to a suspected attacker wallet. The company confirmed the security incident, saying it had identified and fixed the issue affecting its international platform, Polymarket.com, and referred the breach to law enforcement. "One of our third party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement," Polymarket said. "Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading and are working to bring the platform back online." Polymarket initially placed its exchange into cancel-only mode at 2:05 p.m. ET and paused relayer actions while investigating the incident. At 2:37 p.m., the company announced that the issue had been fixed and that trading was temporarily halted out of an abundance of caution. Trading resumed approximately one hour after the initial suspension, with the incident marked resolved at 3:05 p.m. ET. "Trading is now fully back online," the company announced on X. "We'll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders." Polymarket has not disclosed how many users were affected, how much cryptocurrency was stolen, or how the reimbursement process will work. Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified a suspected attacker-controlled wallet (0x3F99139F1C5854bb628c2e576Aaf638e99dFfc18) embedded in the malicious JavaScript. BleepingComputer's examination of the wallet's blockchain activity found that it transferred approximately 28.6 million POL, valued at roughly $2.57 million, to three additional wallets. Blockchain records also show that the wallet conducted numerous transactions involving Polymarket's prediction-market token contract between 1:50 p.m. and 1:56 p.m. ET, shortly before the exchange suspended trading. Hudson Rock reported that the wallet held approximately $2.19 million in cryptocurrency at the time of its investigation. Malicious JavaScript used to drain wallets Security researchers at Hudson Rock identified malicious JavaScript distributed through cdn.debugbear[.]com/C7xcKKrjUnXK.js that was designed to steal cryptocurrency and prediction-market holdings from Polymarket users. The script was hosted on infrastructure belonging to DebugBear, a website performance-monitoring service that helps organizations track website loading speeds and user experience. DebugBear's Real User Monitoring (RUM) service uses JavaScript embedded in websites to collect performance metrics from visitors' browsers. DebugBear has since confirmed that it is investigating an ongoing security incident and warned customers to remove its monitoring JavaScript from their websites. "We're impacted by an ongoing security incident," DebugBear said in a post on X. "If you use our RUM product, please remove the embed code from your website." At the time of writing, DebugBear's website was inaccessible, displaying a Cloudflare error. It is unclear whether the website outage is related to containment efforts or another consequence of the incident. Hudson Rock's researchers also discovered Polymarket production build metadata containing the commit message, "chore(polymarket): remove debugbear rum script (#15337)," indicating that the platform had removed the DebugBear monitoring integration. The build was timestamped October 29 at 1:59 p.m. ET, shortly before Polymarket publicly announced the incident. BleepingComputer analyzed a copy of the malicious JavaScript file (VirusTotal), finding that it was designed to hijack authenticated Polymarket trading sessions, liquidate users' prediction-market positions, and transfer cryptocurrency and other assets to an attacker-controlled wallet. The malware checks whether a visitor is logged into Polymarket and attempts to use their existing trading session and the platform's trading functionality to carry out unauthorized transactions. It then checks the user's cryptocurrency balances and prediction-market positions to determine the value of their holdings. Depending on how the user authenticated to Polymarket, the malware attempts to steal their assets in different ways. For some users, it tries to automatically sell their prediction-market positions. For others, the malware attempts to transfer their prediction-market tokens directly to an attacker-controlled wallet. Malicious JavaScript attempts to transfer users' Polymarket prediction-market tokens to an attacker-controlled wallet Source: BleepingComputer The malware also attempts to convert users' cryptocurrency holdings into assets that can be transferred to an attacker-controlled wallet, using Polymarket's existing transaction functionality. BleepingComputer found that the malicious script communicated with data.debugbear.com to receive instructions and send data about targeted accounts, wallet addresses, balances, and transaction results. The use of DebugBear's infrastructure to both distribute the malicious script and serve as a command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration server raises questions about the how much access the attackers had to the company's systems. BleepingComputer has contacted Polymarket and DebugBear with questions about the incident and will update this article if we receive a response. 38zuuh.text: A fake cryptocurrency trading app called Padre Terminal, previously available on the Apple App Store for iOS devices, has been linked to the theft of approximately $23,000 from 27 Solana wallets. Blockchain investigator Iris confirmed that one victim was compromised through the malicious App Store app, but has not determined how the other affected wallets were compromised. The researcher says the app drains wallets after unsuspecting users import their private keys into it. Padre was a cryptocurrency trading platform, mainly used to buy and sell meme coins on Solana. It was later renamed Terminal by pump.fun, a platform focused on creating, buying, and selling cryptocurrency “meme coins” on the Solana blockchain. Iris says the legitimate Padre trading service, now Terminal by pump.fun, is web-only, so any mobile apps impersonating it, including the one previously available on the App Store, are malicious. At the time of BleepingComputer's initial investigation, we found two Padre apps on the App Store (ID 6802739263 and ID 6717572591). The former was the Iris-confirmed drainer app, while the latter is likely pump.fun's official app, live since October 2024. The malicious crypto drainer app on the App Store Source: BleepingComputer The malicious Padre Terminal app has since been removed from the App Store, with its listing now returning a 404 error. Iris told BleepingComputer it suspects the trading interface of the fake app is served remotely, but has not directly observed the wallet-draining screen. According to Iris, the operation has drained 27 Solana wallets since October 25, 2026, stealing approximately $23,000 in cryptocurrency. The stolen cryptocurrency was traced to the Solana address 3LAgKYoNenWrGWT3U4XWhpgVJWyYkP9wKpiPk8TJT1LN. Iris says the attacker converted all remaining USDC (4,070 tokens) into SOL on October 29, eliminating the possibility of Circle freezing those funds. The attacker then transferred 192 SOL to a new wallet (H84yazsUVCF8eJ6brh27rURMHjdKEVv2BuLS4iuUUQbu). According to Iris, the two wallets held a combined 229.66 SOL, with no funds cashed out at the time of the researcher's update. The drainer remained active after the app's removal, with the latest reported theft occurring at 17:06 UTC on October 29. More suspicious apps on the App Store Iris identified at least five suspected crypto-brand impersonators on the App Store, including Padre Terminal, Axiom Pro: Focus, GMGN AI, HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools, and Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs. Their listings feature seemingly harmless descriptions, but user reviews below sometimes reveal their true nature, with many exposing them for wallet theft and scams. The Axiom Pro: Focus app, for example, had approximately 25 user reviews alleging wallet theft since February. One reviewer claimed the app had presented itself as a meme coin trading platform before changing into a focus application. A review of the GMGN AI app alleged that $2,000 had been stolen, while a review associated with HyperTerminal-HyperliquidTools reported the theft of $2,020. Another app, Pump Fun Tokens & Analitycs, presented itself as a notes application but had a review explicitly accusing it of stealing cryptocurrency. Two suspicious apps Iris discovered on the App Store Source: BleepingComputer.com Iris also found a script on the fake Axiom website containing backend addresses associated with Axiom, Aster, and GMGN impersonators, suggesting a common operator. However, Padre Terminal was not linked to that cluster. Also, a script on the GMGN website blocks visitors from several CIS countries, potentially indicating that the attackers are attempting to avoid targeting users in those regions. Iris has not independently confirmed cryptocurrency theft for the four suspicious apps. BleepingComputer has contacted Apple about the Padre drainer and the other four suspicious apps available on the App Store, but we have not heard back as of publication. In March 2024, a fake Leather cryptocurrency wallet app appeared on the Apple App Store, and multiple users reported losing their assets after connecting their wallets to it. Apple eventually removed the app two weeks later and blocked the publisher from its developer program. Users are recommended to follow links to the App Store from the projects' official websites and avoid installing apps with only a handful of downloads and reviews, or those published by entities with names that appear completely unrelated to the project. 1vjops2.text: Some attacks take real skill. Others just need someone to leave a door open. This week has both. Exposed passwords, old bugs still getting exploited, and trusted software doing things it shouldn't.There's a strange mix of clever tricks and careless mistakes. Hackers are borrowing trust from familiar apps, websites, and AI tools. Some are using AI to speed things up. Others are leaving their own attack files exposed. Not exactly careful work.Different stories, familiar weak spots. Here's what showed up this week.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. PHP2Shell attacks persist WordPress security company Wordefence said it's not aware of any WordPress site compromised through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) as of October 28, 2026. "We continue to see PHP2Shell-related requests across the more than 5 million sites we protect," it said. "Those requests show ongoing scanning and exploitation attempts; they do not show whether an attempt succeeded. Our site-cleaning and incident response teams have not handled a WordPress compromise attributed to these vulnerabilities." 40,573 secrets exposed Hudson Rock's investigation into the FortiBleed credential harvesting campaign has uncovered 975 newly identified domains and 40,573 exposed secrets, including 37,076 local-user records and 1,576 Active Directory LDAP bind records. The data comes from newly obtained 1,703 FortiGate source files associated with 1,689 host identifiers. "The configuration material dates to around February 2026, earlier than the likely May/June material examined in the first investigation," Hudson Rock said. The latest discovery has been codenamed FortiBleed 2.0. Institutional DNS hijacked Threat actors have used domain shadowing to place illegal gambling content beneath legitimate school and government domains in two unrelated operations. "In both cases, an unauthorized party appears to have gained access to DNS administration and created records that the original domain owners may not have noticed," Infoblox said. "Because the resulting hostnames sat within established institutional namespaces, they provided especially useful infrastructure for search-engine optimization (SEO) and traffic acquisition." One cluster, linked to a threat actor called Hidden Hawk, has been found to add individual CNAME records that mapped institutional hostnames to gambling pages hosted largely on Cloudflare Pages. The second campaign exploiting an Indian government domain "delegated entire subzones to third-party authoritative nameservers and used a wildcard, allowing many hostnames to be managed outside the victim's DNS environment." Put differently, the unauthorized DNS access creates new institutional hostnames, which resolve to infrastructure serving illegal gambling doorway pages. The pages also leverage the established reputation of school and government namespaces to ensure that the malicious URLs show up prominently in search engine results. AI banking credential warning Bank of America is reminding customers not to share banking credentials with AI agents. In an email blast to customers titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," the financial institution urged customers to never share their username and password with another person or an outside service, "including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on your behalf." Android tightens contact access Google has announced that an upcoming Android release will no longer be able to directly write to contacts with the WRITE_CONTACTS permission. "Instead, you can use the standard contact intents (ACTION_INSERT, ACTION_EDIT, and ACTION_INSERT_OR_EDIT)," Google said. "Currently, if your app needs to save even one contact, you might be requesting WRITE_CONTACTS. But that permission grants broad access, allowing an app to make widespread changes to contacts across the device in the background, even without user interaction. Most apps don’t need such broad permission." 26,400 live credentials exposed A scan of 7.25 million public repositories on Gitee, China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform, has uncovered 26,400 unique verified-live credentials, including an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys, independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann said. Critical Fortinet fixes released Fortinet has released a "coordinated set of security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer" to address critical and high-severity flaws that were flagged using an AI-assisted vulnerability discovery approach. Details of the issues are being kept under wraps until November 10, 2026. With Fortinet devices becoming a favorite target for attackers, it's essential that users move quickly to apply the fixes. Zero-permission token theft Details have emerged about a now-patched flaw in Microsoft Authenticator (CVE-2026-80097 aka AuthMask) that could be exploited by installing and running a malicious application on an affected Android device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in the app by claiming to be a trusted app and getting the corresponding tokens. The flaw could be exploited to take over work accounts without requiring additional permissions. "Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to obtain authentication tokens and access resources as the affected user," Microsoft said. According to Enclave, "an unprivileged Android app with zero permissions could impersonate any installed Microsoft first-party app and have the Microsoft Authenticator broker hand it that app's tokens. The setup is a device with Authenticator installed and one work account signed into it." 32 fake AI bots hunt secrets Attackers are disguising themselves as AI agents to steal credentials. Cequence said it has tracked a single actor running AI agent impersonation at scale by posing as about 32 different AI bots, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Perplexity, while searching for passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. "The malicious scanner runs from a major cloud provider and rotates through about 32 AI bot identities, spanning crawlers and assistants from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Perplexity, and others," Will Glazier said. "It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths. Each address sends a short burst of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds and then moves on. The scanner works through targets one at a time, around the clock, and first sends random nonsense paths to find websites that answer every request, a common scanning technique. It hit organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software, and stayed active from at least late September through late October." China-linked network intrusion The U.S. Embassy in Fiji has revealed that hackers linked to China broke into a regional organization based in Suva between July and August 2026. "Hackers with links to China maintained access to the organization's network over several days," it said. The embassy did not name the threat actor. Nor did it disclose what data the attackers may have accessed. Camera software weaponized Attackers have been breaking into enterprise networks via camera management software, according to new research from security firm Huntress, which observed multiple incidents in September and October 2026 and traced them back to a compromised application. Source code artifacts point to a Korean company selling analog and IP cameras and digital and network video recorders. The activity abuses the legitimate "WpcMon.exe" binary to sideload DLLs that establish outbound connections to a remote server. "This activity demonstrates how attackers can blend malicious code with trusted Windows components to evade detection," Huntress said. 68 GB government data breach In a major operational security blunder, an unknown threat actor stole 68 GB from a Philippine government agency, maintained a detailed log of the transfer, then left that log open on the internet at 13.163.205[.]35:80. "The copy finished in under 24 minutes on September 6, 2026," Hunt.io said. "The transfer log records 27 SQL Server backups whose filenames correspond to the case-management systems of a Philippine overseas-employment and migrant-worker administration. Beside the log sat the operator's toolkit, a rebranded GodPotato build, a PowerShell stager, two payloads and a full Impacket environment." AI model data exfiltration concerns Canadian AI company Cohere has claimed that it caught Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model unsuccessfully attempting to send data to China from its evaluation sandbox as part of a prompt instructing the LLM to detect malicious file download and execution by monitoring for curl processes downloading bash scripts to /tmp followed by bash execution. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," Cohere said. "We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training." Cohere has also released a dataset containing the model trace and corresponding raw token IDs in connection with the behavior. "The exact output is not guaranteed all the time, and many trials may be required to reproduce the behavior," Cohere said, adding "there are similarly unexpected URLs that the model also tends to output, most containing aliyunc." However, the findings have also led to social media chatter that the company is resorting to geopolitical fearmongering and that they are an attempt to clamp down on open-weights models. Post-quantum migration roadmap The U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has released guidelines that detail the timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. "The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another," said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. "We understand there's not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what's changing." AI-powered ransomware operation exposed SOCRadar has uncovered the live workspace (i.e., open directory) of a threat actor tied to the n0n ransomware group, which exposed the operation's full workflow as of September 2026. The directory at 185.157.161[.]148 includes an AI coding agent configured with about 150 models to produce hundreds of attack scripts, with more than $7,216 in usage costs. "Entry points included a credential stuffing campaign against 305 FortiGate SSL-VPN devices, exposed AWS keys, weak RDP/WinRM credentials, and compromised hosting management portals," SOCRadar said. At least 23 organizations across 14 countries are said to have been identified in the workspace, including a U.S. sports retailer, a cloud provider, a teachers’ union, a Venezuelan ISP, an Argentine ministry and a pharmaceutical subsidiary. Government AI access restricted The Swedish government has barred employees from accessing browser-based versions of ChatGPT or Claude on their work computers over security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data. "Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training," Euro News reported. 42 repositories hijacked JFrog and SafeDep have uncovered a campaign in which threat actors hijacked third-party 42 GitHub repositories across 11 owners to deploy payload blobs large enough "to evade the GitHub search and API paths normally used to find this kind of compromise." JFrog said, "The repositories contain execution hooks for AI coding assistants and IDEs, plus 12.9 to 13.7 MB polymorphic wrappers that all decode to the same hidden CI-publisher payload." The activity is assessed to be related to a Miasma-family npm worm propagated under various packages ending with "testmetest." According to SafeDep, the worm "shares code with Miasma 'Phantom Gyp' from June 2026 and adds the token-revocation wiper from Mini Shai-Hulud. The malicious versions steal credentials, spread to other packages and repositories, and install a wiper that deletes the home directory when the victim revokes the stolen GitHub token." Unsuspecting developers who installed the packages had their data stolen and repositories compromised with malicious code to produce further malicious testmetest releases and run shellpanel workflows targeting cPanel systems through CVE-2026-41940, overlapping with a prior campaign detailed by Socket in July 2026. Android banking malware-as-a-service A new Android malware operation called MR ROBOT is targeting customers of Indian banks and transforming banking fraud into a subscription business, with cybercriminals renting customized banking trojans to steal OTPs, card details, UPI PINs and credentials while secretly forwarding calls to bypass security checks. "It is not a single-actor campaign but a rented crimeware platform: a master operator leases access to affiliates, who use a Telegram bot ('APK Shield) and a web control panel (v7.0) to build personalized banking trojans on demand and distribute them through fake Play-Store-style pages and messaging-app lures," CloudSEK said. The kit impersonates around 36 lure apps, including banks, utility providers, and government services. One affiliate is estimated to have intercepted 5407 text messages from 153 infected devices. MDM platforms abused for remote access Threat actors are abusing legitimate mobile device management (MDM) platforms, like Hexnode and Rippling, by using social engineering to enroll devices or install management agents, per Huntress. "Once established, MDM provides a trusted, privileged path for malicious activity, such as deploying rogue RMM tools and maintaining remote access," it said. Critical Gotenberg RCE exploited Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-42589 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical remote code execution flaw in Gotenberg, to deliver a Go-based reverse shell called "cache_base." The flaw was patched in May 2026. According to VulnCheck, the activity originated from a residential Japanese IP address in early October 2026. "The execution flow is straightforward: acquire a lock, collect host information, connect to C2, register the victim, and open a shell," VulnCheck said. Over the past 30 days, the vulnerability has recorded 1,358 exploitation events from 128 unique source IP addresses. Discord discussions go public Discord has announced it will allow search engines to index discussions in Discoverable Servers and make them accessible on the web to users outside the platform without an account or invitation, starting mid-December 2026. "Discussions in Discoverable Servers will soon be easier to find when you search the web, so you can find the answer you're looking for and step straight into the conversation on Discord," it said. The changes apply only to Discoverable Servers and do not extend to private servers and direct messages. 800+ ransomware victims claimed The Gentlemen ransomware operation has claimed more than 800 victims across multiple regions and sectors, with most attacks targeting organizations in the U.S. and Europe. "The group supports multiple platforms, with ransomware variants targeting Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD systems, allowing its affiliates to target a broad range of enterprise environments," Acronis said. "The group's operations include the use of EDR-killing tools. In a recent incident, a custom dropper was observed deploying vulnerable Safetica ProcessMonitorDriver [CVE-2025-70795] and Lenovo BootRepair.sys drivers to terminate security processes." AI model loading RCE risk Pillar Security has disclosed an arbitrary-code-execution vulnerability in Unsloth's core model-loading path (CVE-2026-93348, CVSS score: 8.6). It has been fixed in unsloth_zoo 2026.8.14. "An attacker-controlled model configuration could cause Python code to execute during loading," researcher Ariel Fogel said. "The affected code ran inside the model-loading process, with access to whatever that process could read, modify, or authenticate to. In an AI development environment, that can include proprietary datasets, model artifacts, Hugging Face tokens, and cloud credentials. Exploitation required an affected loading path to process an attacker-controlled configuration." Unauthenticated root-level RCE XBOW said it identified an unauthenticated, critical-severity remote code execution bug in a public web application belonging to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission (EAC). "The vulnerable application was a resource/logistics calculator, not a voting machine or voter registration system," XBOW researcher Ariel Walter Garcia said. "The flaw allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute code as root inside the backend container, with access to locally protected resources and outbound network connectivity, a privileged foothold reachable via a crafted unauthenticated web request." Session-hijacking RAT emerges A new remote access trojan called DarkCore comes with a dedicated browser that could let attackers access Gmail, WhatsApp, and MediaFire accounts using stolen sessions, while giving the impression that the activity is originating from the victim's own IP address. DarkCore was first advertised on cybercrime forums in August 2026. "The seller describes a browser that reuses those sessions to access work mailboxes, instant messaging apps, cloud storage and other services through the infected machine's IP address," BlackFog said. "The purpose is to make the access look like legitimate activity from the user." AI-powered malware framework Cisco Talos has disclosed details of a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework called NIK C2. The implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. "NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim's sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session," Talos said. "In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is an HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies." Three different versions of the malware have been identified to date since August 12, 2026. Talos said NIK C2 alters adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session. Malicious PDF delivers backdoor A phishing email using a FedEx tax invoice lure and containing a ZIP archive with a PDF has been observed triggering a multi-stage infection process to deliver a previously undocumented variant of the Sirius Backdoor. "The PDF abuses /OpenAction and /Launch objects to trigger an embedded Base64-encoded PowerShell command upon opening," Trellix said. "Execution relies on social engineering to trick the user into approving the PDF reader's security confirmation prompt. jfx5l8.text: A newly identified advanced persistent threat (APT) group tracked as UAT-11473 was observed exploiting CVE-2026-20127, an authentication-bypass flaw in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controllers, to deploy a custom malware framework called KeyDrift. CVE-2026-20127 is a max-severity flaw that Cisco patched in February 2026, which allows remote attackers to gain privileged access to Catalyst SD-WAN Controller and Manager and add rogue peers. UAT-8616 has exploited the vulnerability as a zero-day since at least 2023, and recent research also linked its exploitation to the Chinese Volt Typhoon state-sponsored hacking group. According to Cisco Talos researchers who reported on the activity, the UAT-11473 threat cluster appears to overlap with Volt Typhoon’s "Silent Train" covert access network, but they made no definitive links. In a report Lumen released yesterday, researchers revealed that the Silent Train framework allowed Volt Typhoon to evade detection while conducting zero-day vulnerability attacks. Deploying KeyDrift The attacks Cisco researchers observed targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research organizations, using the KeyDrift malware, which is a custom malware framework designed to operate on Cisco SD-WAN controller instances. "Talos assesses with high confidence that the framework is designed to provide long-term persistent access and automated exfiltration of sensitive keying material," explained Cisco Talos. "KeyDrift operates inside SD-WAN control-plane processes and is capable of intercepting decrypted control traffic, extracting control-session metadata and data-plane keying material, and staging or transmitting the collected material using encrypted records." KeyDrift has two primary components, PolyFlame and LittleFilch, for which Talos saw signs of ongoing development, including new anti-debugging mechanisms and varied process impersonation. PolyFlame runs inside legitimate vdaemon processes using modified service startup scripts and an injector for deployment. It supports command execution through a TinyShell-styled component, file uploads and downloads, and relaying communications between an attacker’s command-and-control (C2) server and multiple peers. LittleFilch is a control-session interception module that hooks SSL_read to inspect control-plane messages after they have been decrypted inside the controller. For predefined edge nodes, it extracts IP identifiers and a 32-byte field that Talos assesses to be AES-256 IPsec data-plane key material. It uses RSA encryption to protect the collected information, saves it to /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, and then transmits it over UDP to the attackers. Talos believes with high confidence that KeyDrift is designed to maintain persistent access to Cisco SD-WAN controllers, intercept control-plane traffic, extract cryptographic keys, and securely stage or exfiltrate the stolen data. Cisco recommends that system administrators apply the available security updates for CVE-2026-20127 and also consult the vendor’s dedicated hardening guide for Catalyst SD-WAN deployments. aazz8w.text: A massive search-hijacking campaign involving 319 Chrome extensions with a combined 13.4 million reported installations redirected users' searches through tracking servers to generate advertising revenue from Bing and Yahoo. A new report by Socket's John Tuckner expands on the researcher's April 2025 discovery of 57 Chrome extensions with 6 million users, adding 264 newly identified add-ons with another 8.7 million users. "These extensions were created by a handful of organized operators all working from the same idea: quietly take over the browser's default search engine, route every query through a suspicious proxy server, and collect partner referral payments from Yahoo or Bing under a syndication partner ID," explained Tuckner. The extensions, with the full list shared at the bottom of Socket's report, pretend to be PDF converters, manual finders, safe search, and AI search tools. However, for the most part, the extensions simply redirect users' searches through a series of sites until they land on Bing or Yahoo. Although they are hosted on the Chrome Web Store, Google's official portal for Chrome add-ons, Socket says they are unlisted and don't appear in users' searches on the extension store. Instead, the extensions are promoted through shady advertisements found on websites. Tuckner explains that many of these extensions need almost no code to achieve their goal, as Chrome's built-in 'chrome_settings_overrides' setting allows them to replace the default search provider. One example analyzed in the report includes only a manifest and icons, with no background scripts, content scripts, or requested permissions. Browser-hijacking extensions like these have long blurred the line between potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) and malware, with BleepingComputer reporting on hundreds of similar extensions over the years. Risk extends beyond ad fraud The extensions currently focus on revenue generation through search referrals, passing user searches through an operator-controlled server before they reach Yahoo or Bing. However, Tuckner warns that the final destination can change at any time without updating the extension, including redirecting users to phishing sites or malicious downloads. "The search referral revenue is a profitable watering hole while the proxy operator can wait for data to accumulate and targets to surface before redirecting to malicious search results or landing pages for phishing or other malicious downloads," explains Tuckner. An example of this is the Predator Search extension, which redirected Tuckner to four different sites when performing six identical searches. "Six identical searches sent through its proxy search server ended in four different places: straight to Yahoo with partner tags (hspart=sz&hsimp=yhs-026), a landing page on searchlio.net, a hop through searchtosearch.com to a second results domain (mcftink.com) before Yahoo, and a Cloudflare non-responsive error page," Tuckner reported. "The extension never changed; the proxy chose each destination as the search came in." The largest recently active cluster of extensions is "Bing-Search," with 37 extensions and 2.2 million users, often promoted through Bidbrain ads. Another one is the "SecuryBrowse" wave, with 58 extensions and 4.9 million users, promoting security-themed add-ons like Fire Shield, Securify, and WatchTower. The researcher said most of these extensions had been removed from the Chrome Web Store when the report was published. However, new ones are constantly being added. Users should uninstall the extensions listed in Socket's report from their web browsers, run a full AV scan on their systems, and avoid downloading unnecessary tools and browser add-ons from unknown publishers. BleepingComputer has contacted Google for a comment on Socket's findings, but we have not received a response by publication. fj9ffk.text: A flaw in the Linux kernel's TCP code, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), and other Linux distributions. The kernel's own CVE team rates it 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Anthropic said on October 27 that its AI model wrote an exploit that uses the flaw to let a remote attacker with no credentials run commands as root on Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener. As of October 29, Ubuntu and RHEL have not released a fixed kernel. Red Hat, Amazon, Oracle, and SUSE score the flaw between 5.9 and 8.1, lower than the kernel team's 9.8. The flaw is a race condition in the code that sets up new IPv4 TCP connections. It can make the kernel read memory it has already freed, a bug type known as a use-after-free. The kernel fix credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge with reporting the bug. Neither the CVE record nor the fix mentions multipath TCP (MPTCP). The link between that feature and this bug comes from Anthropic's post. MPTCP lets one connection use several network paths at once. On Linux, an application must request MPTCP when it opens a socket. Anthropic's post says the flaw "was patched upstream and backported to all maintained stable kernel branches." For distribution users, that fix arrives only in the vendor's kernel package. Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux have shipped fixed packages, at least for some of their kernels, but Ubuntu and RHEL have not. Which Distributions Have a Fix Distribution Vendor rating Status as of October 29 Fixed package or advisory Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, 26.04 LTS and 26.10 Priority High Work in progress None released Ubuntu 16.04, 18.04 and 20.04 Priority High Vulnerable None released RHEL 8, 9 and 10, OpenShift 4 Moderate, 5.9 (CVE page) Important, 8.1 ( advisory file) Fix deferred None released RHEL 7 Not applicable Not affected Not needed Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.18 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 24 kernel6.18-6.18.56-125.164.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3251) Amazon Linux 2023, kernel6.12 package Important, 7.0 Fixed October 29 in Amazon's advisory; Amazon's CVE page still says pending kernel6.12-6.12.113-138.209.amzn2023 (ALAS2023-2026-3335) Amazon Linux 2 Amazon Linux 2023, kernel package Important, 7.0 Pending fix None released Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9 and 10, UEK kernel Important, 8.1 Fixed October 16 ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, ELSA-2026-500399 Debian trixie (stable) No score listed Fixed October 16 linux 6.12.113-1 (DSA-6568-1) Debian 12 (bookworm) No score listed Fixed October 17 and October 22 linux 6.1.190-1 (DLA-4841-1) linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1 (DLA-4850-1) SUSE Linux Micro 6.2, openSUSE Leap 16.0 Important, 8.1 Fixed kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1 or later SLES 15 SP4 to SP6 LTSS, SLES 16.0, SLE Micro 5.3 to 5.5 Important, 8.1 In testing None released SLES 15 SP7 Important, 8.1 Affected, fix in progress None released Ubuntu also lists its cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernels as vulnerable or as work in progress. Red Hat says its fixes are "currently deferred to a future update." Neither Red Hat nor Ubuntu gives a release date. How the Bug Works The race happens during the TCP handshake. When a connection is completed, the kernel hands the IP options stored with the pending request to the new socket without copying them. If that socket is destroyed while another CPU is still using the options to answer a resent connection request, the kernel reads freed memory. IPv6 is not affected by this race because the kernel copies the options for IPv6 connections. The bug was introduced in Linux 4.4. Kernel developers applied a fix on October 5, ten days before the CVE was published. The fix makes the kernel wait until other CPUs finish reading the options before it frees them. Why the Scores Differ The kernel's CVE team added the 9.8 score to the CVE record on October 24, nine days after publishing the CVE. Its score assumes an attacker who sends a TCP connection request carrying IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options, then resends the request to try to win the race. The team rated attack complexity low, saying both sides of the race are "attacker-induced." In that case, the team says, the bug could send nearby kernel memory back to the attacker, corrupt kernel memory, or crash the system. As of October 28, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) had not added its own score and showed the kernel team's 9.8. Ubuntu's page also shows that score. Red Hat's CVE page rates the flaw Moderate, scoring it 5.9 because the race is hard to win. It says the most likely result is a kernel crash, with memory corruption possible in theory, and that "no confidentiality or integrity impact has been demonstrated." Red Hat's machine-readable advisory file, updated on October 29, lists the impact as Important and scores the flaw 8.1, with high confidentiality and integrity impact. Red Hat's bug tracker changed the issue's severity from medium to high the same day. On that day, the CVE page showed Moderate and 5.9. Oracle and SUSE also score the flaw 8.1, with the same CVSS vector as Red Hat's advisory file. Those scores match the kernel team's on every metric except attack complexity, which the vendors rate high and the kernel team rates low. Amazon scores it 7.0. What Anthropic Says It Built Anthropic described the Linux exploit in an October 27 post about flaws that its AI model, Claude, found and exploited. The Hacker News covered the post on October 28. Claude wrote the exploit after "initial prompting," Anthropic said. The exploit works in two stages. First, the race makes the kernel send extra bytes back to the attacker. Once one of those replies contains a kernel address, the attacker can get around KASLR, the kernel's memory address randomization. Second, the same bug overflows a buffer and overwrites a callback pointer with the address of a payload the attacker had already placed in kernel memory. When the kernel calls that pointer, the payload executes a shell command of the attacker's choice as root. A lost race only fails that one connection attempt and does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep trying, the company said. In its test, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes, and reaching command execution took 5 more minutes. The post does not include the exploit code, the kernel version, or the configuration Anthropic tested. Red Hat says a remote attacker who can reach an exposed TCP service could trigger the race. Anthropic's root exploit, however, targeted servers with a multipath TCP listener. The post does not say whether servers without one can be taken over the same way. As of October 29, none of the vendor advisories, the CVE record, or Anthropic's post reports attacks using the flaw. It does not appear in a copy of CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog that Luxembourg's CIRCL last updated on October 28. What to Do Now Where your distribution has released a fixed kernel, install it. The table above lists the packages and advisories for Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE and Amazon Linux. If you build your own kernel, the fix is in Linux 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3. The kernel's CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel. It says the kernel community does not support cherry-picking individual fixes. Ubuntu, RHEL and some Amazon Linux and SUSE releases have no fixed kernel to install yet. Red Hat says no available mitigation meets its standards for being easy to deploy, suitable for most installations and stable. None of the other vendor advisories lists one. The advisories and Anthropic's post do not say whether turning off multipath TCP, or blocking incoming connection requests that carry IP options, would lower the risk.

rkdzos.text: Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba. The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader. "The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis. To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google. Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below - github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop gpt-5-6.github[.]io github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io opus-5-0[.]github[.]io "Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone." Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components - Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment. Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks. YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData." The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload. The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks - Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub"). Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io." Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input. Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat"). "By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said. The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner. Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions. "The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."

yotknl.text: Microsoft has resolved a known issue that prevents non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled. When Administrator protection is enabled, it prompts standard users to authenticate with Windows Hello (PIN or biometric) when they try to change the Windows Registry or install new apps. This feature began rolling out in October 2025 and is now enabled by default in organizations using Windows security baselines after installing the October 2026 Windows security update. Microsoft acknowledged on October 13 that Remote Desktop connections may fail with error 0xC000000D after installing the KB5124010 September 2026 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then) on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later. "This issue primarily affects enterprise-managed remote devices used as Remote Desktop hosts with Administrator protection enabled, regardless of how the feature was enabled," it said. Remote Desktop connection failures now fixed On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue is fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update. "This issue was resolved by Windows updates released October 28, 2026 (KB5127936), and later," it noted. "We recommend you install the latest security update for your device as it contains important improvements and issue resolutions, including this one." Microsoft also provides a temporary workaround for users who don't want to install this preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates, which requires IT administrators to disable the admin protection feature by resetting the "User Account Control Type Of Admin Approval Mode" policy via Microsoft Intune or Group Policy. Microsoft fixed a similar issue in March 2025 that was causing Remote Desktop and RDS connection failures after installing Windows updates released since January 2025. It also released emergency out-of-band Windows updates last month to fix Remote Desktop Services failures caused by the September 2026 security updates. b2sg4z.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybersecurity Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. "It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55). One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon. Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection. The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program. Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing. The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks." "GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said. "GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task." Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software. This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft. "These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said. "These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

1kwmvaz.text: The Hacker NewsOct 29, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Webinar Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act. Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle. The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first. That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation. Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action. Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first? When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process. The webinar focuses on two practical needs: broad visibility and faster action. Security teams need enough context to understand risk across cloud infrastructure, code, identities, SaaS, AI services, and the software supply chain. They also need a way to identify exploitable paths, investigate suspicious activity, and deliver remediation to the right owner without having to rebuild the same context every time. A Wiz expert will explain how organizations can use unified security context to separate urgent exposure from background noise, understand attack paths, and bring security agents into investigation and remediation workflows. For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it. The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership. Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. The key questions are practical: Can you see enough of the environment to understand an attack path? Can you quickly determine whether a new issue affects something attackers can reach? Can you move a validated risk from detection to remediation fast enough? AI is increasing the speed at which weaknesses can be found and used. Security teams need to respond with better context and less delay.

14ic6cu.text: A flaw in Telegram for Android allowed an attacker to run code on a victim's phone via a voice call once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec. The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29. The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, NebuSec's co-founder and chief executive said in an email to The Hacker News. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026. The company confirmed it in private phone calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls. Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29. The Hacker News has asked NebuSec and Telegram whether the flaw was used in real attacks, and asked NebuSec what an attacker's code could reach on a phone. During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated. The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec. Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field. Version 12.10.4 reads the rotation value from the right field. The calling code that uses this message was switched on in version 8.6.2, the first version NebuSec names. Telegram's Android, iOS, and desktop apps use one shared library, called tgcalls, for calls. A change labeled "Fix camera rotation" made the same correction in tgcalls on April 21, 2026. Telegram's iOS source code included that change from version 12.7, released in May, and the desktop app's code from version 7.0.1, released in July. Telegram for Android received it in version 12.10.4 in September. Whether the earlier code could be exploited in those apps has not been shown. NebuSec's video shows two phones, one marked as the attacker and one as the victim. The victim accepts a Telegram call. About half a minute into the call, the victim's phone switches to its home screen, the app icons fall down the screen, and a "HACKED BY NEBUSEC" logo appears. The video does not show which Telegram or Android version the victim's phone was running.
