How AI is making fake login pages more convincing Attackers have long used fake login pages to steal credentials, but generative AI makes it easier to create convincing replicas of legitimate authentication portals. From company logos and page layouts to login prompts, these fraudulent pages can closely resemble the websites employees regularly access. AI also makes it easier to tailor phishing campaigns to specific organizations or employees. For example, attackers can create personalized IT notifications that direct employees to a fraudulent login page using the company's branding and familiar authentication prompts. These attacks often rely on lookalike domains that closely resemble legitimate web addresses, with subtle spelling changes or additional characters. Combined with realistic login pages and targeted messaging, these tactics make phishing attempts harder to recognize. While these techniques aren't new, generative AI lets attackers create, customize and adapt phishing campaigns more quickly and at a larger scale. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report found that phishing accounted for 44% of the AI-assisted initial-access techniques examined. How fake login pages lead to account takeovers Fake login pages can capture more than usernames and passwords. Some replicate multi-step authentication processes to collect MFA codes, which attackers can attempt to use before they expire to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts and applications. More sophisticated attacks use Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) techniques to intercept authentication sessions. In these attacks, a fraudulent website acts as a proxy between the user and the legitimate service, relaying authentication requests in real time. After the user successfully authenticates, the attacker may capture a session cookie or authentication token and use it to access the account without completing another MFA challenge. This makes session hijacking particularly dangerous. Even with MFA enabled, attackers can potentially access accounts by stealing active session tokens. This lets them hijack an authenticated session without entering a password or completing another MFA challenge. Why traditional phishing defenses aren't always enough Security awareness training helps employees recognize phishing attempts, but convincing login page replicas can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate websites. Even experienced users can overlook subtle warning signs, particularly when a fraudulent page uses familiar branding and authentication prompts. Email filters, URL blocklists and website reputation services can stop many known phishing threats, but newly registered domains and short-lived phishing sites may evade detection. Attackers also distribute malicious links through text messages, collaboration platforms and search ads, letting phishing attempts bypass email-based defenses. URL inspection provides another layer of protection, but lookalike domains can be difficult to identify. A valid HTTPS connection also doesn't guarantee that a website is legitimate. These gaps highlight the need for security controls that can evaluate suspicious websites and detect potential credential-harvesting attempts before users enter their login information. How organizations can protect against credential theft Organizations can reduce the risk of credential theft by strengthening authentication, detecting suspicious login pages and limiting what attackers can access if an account is compromised. Use phishing-resistant MFA and passkeys: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use cryptographic authentication tied to legitimate website domains, reducing the risk of credential theft through fraudulent login pages. Implement browser-level phishing protection: Browser-based security tools can detect look-alike domains, brand impersonation and suspicious URL patterns. AI-powered detection can help identify credential-harvesting sites and warn users before they enter sensitive information. Monitor authentication and session activity: Unusual sign-in locations, unfamiliar devices and suspicious session behavior can indicate account compromise. Continuous monitoring helps security teams identify and respond to potential account takeovers. Limit privileged access: Enforcing least-privilege policies and removing unnecessary standing privileges limits what attackers can access through compromised accounts. Just-in-time access further reduces the window of opportunity for abusing elevated permissions. Establish phishing response procedures: Organizations should have clear processes for reporting suspected phishing attempts, revoking compromised sessions, resetting credentials and investigating unauthorized access. Protecting credentials before they're exposed Phishing protection needs to extend beyond email filters and traditional detection methods to the point where users enter their credentials. Keeper's AI-powered Phishing Protection uses on-device AI to identify suspicious websites, including look-alike domains and spoofed login pages, warning users before they enter their credentials. By identifying suspicious websites earlier, organizations can reduce opportunities for credential harvesting and prevent stolen credentials from leading to account takeovers. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

12obxc8.text: The North Korea-linked Lazarus Group has been attributed to a cyber espionage campaign dubbed Operation FlashHole targeting at least three organizations in South Korea spanning the construction, software, and wire-communication equipment manufacturing sectors. According to Russian cybersecurity company Kaspersky, the campaign has been active since at least July 2025. It's assessed to pick up from where Operation SyncHole left off. "The group targeted victims more selectively, sending spear‑phishing emails with links to fabricated but relevant sites, such as portfolio and résumé pages tailored to each target," Sojun Ryu, senior security researcher at Kaspersky GReAT, said in an exhaustive analysis. Operation SyncHole was first documented by Kaspersky in April 2025, detailing the state-sponsored adversary's targeting of South Korea's software, IT, financial, semiconductor manufacturing, and telecommunications industries since November 2024 to deliver malware such as ThreatNeedle, AGAMEMNON, wAgent, SIGNBT, and COPPERHEDGE. The attacks were characterized by the exploitation of a security flaw in iniLINE Cross EX for malware delivery. Cross EX is a mandatory financial security software program installed by South Korean internet users on their computers to support security software across various browser environments when accessing online banking and government services. The exploit was designed to launch the legitimate "SyncHost.exe" process and inject shellcode into it to load the ThreatNeedle backdoor. The attack chain also incorporated a one-day vulnerability in the Innorix Agent file transfer solution version 9.2.18.496 for lateral movement. Operation FlashHole continues the prior wave's targeting of South Korea-focused software to breach targets. Where SyncHole exploited Cross EX, FlashHole has been found to abuse Initech's INISAFE CrossWeb EX, another mandatory financial security solution necessary to access online banking and government portals in the country. According to iniLINE's website, the company entered into a strategic alliance with Initech as far back as 2010 to develop CrossWeb. It's currently marketed by Initech as a certificate-based authentication and electronic-signature solution. That said, the Lazarus Group has a long history of abusing this software to meet its goals. In Q3 2021, it was used to deploy a downloader named Racket in connection with a long-running campaign called DeathNote. Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise Between 2022 and 2023, AhnLab also disclosed attacks in which the threat actor exploited a security flaw in the software to distribute DLL malware ("SCSKAppLink.dll") via watering hole attacks, with the DLL payload retrieved from IIS web servers compromised by the threat actor. "The group first hacks Korean websites and modifies the content provided from the site," AhnLab noted in a July 2023 report. "When a system using a vulnerable version of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V6 visits this website via a web browser, the Lazarus malware (SCSKAppLink.dll) is installed from the distribution site through the INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe vulnerability." Initial infection chain The findings also come against the backdrop of a joint July 2026 advisory published by the Korea Internet and Security Agency (KISA) and domestic cybersecurity vendors, highlighting the Lazarus Group's exploitation of vulnerabilities in such financial security programs like AnySign4PC to distribute backdoors like Struggle (aka SIGNBT 3.0) and Brandoor (aka COPPERHEDGE) after tricking victims into visiting malicious URLs through spear-phishing and watering hole techniques. "The attackers induced targets to access malicious URLs through various methods, including watering hole and spear-phishing attacks, and then exploited the vulnerabilities to ultimately install backdoor malware," AhnLab said, calling the campaign Operation Double Barrel. The precise initial access vector for FlashHole is unclear, but signs point to malicious websites hosted on GitHub pages, one version of which hosted the résumé of a senior network appliance developer along with a profile photo likely generated using artificial intelligence (AI). Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence It's suspected that targets are sent spear-phishing emails containing links to the malicious site, visiting which triggers an infection sequence involving CrossWeb EX to launch the legitimate Windows binary "fsquirt.exe," which is then used to launch a malicious DLL called TechHub via DLL sideloading. "The infection chain is rather complex and reveals the Lazarus Group's advanced operational techniques on targeted hosts," Kaspersky said. "These techniques conceal their malicious payloads, intent, and their sophisticated malware delivery framework." "Significantly, the execution chain below exists only in memory during the initial infiltration, highlighting the attackers' considerable efforts to hide the initial compromise." TechHub, for its part, downloads from GitHub a malware called TouchHub, which leverages a DLL sideloading a second to launch a rogue DLL payload dubbed TOUCHSHIFT ("mscoree.dll") for setting up persistence by kicking off the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance. Overlaps between Lazarus Group Attacks This second TechHub instance retrieves another malware family known as ClientHub to download and load LPEClient into memory. LPEClient serves as a conduit for Cubridge, the orchestration component of the malware framework designed to fetch various plugins, modules, and tools. Additional details about the malware toolset is as follows - TechHub, an advanced version of the CLOUDBURST and NickelLoader downloader that communicates with GitHub to fetch additional payloads like TouchHub and ClientHub, as well as collect information about the device and its running processes. Cubridge, an improved version of SIDESHOW and LightlessCan capable of communicating with a command-and-control (C2) server and downloading reusable plugins, DLL utilities for one-off tasks, and additional modules to expand its functionality, thereby allowing it to gather comprehensive system information, run commands, and steal files and web browser data. It's also assessed to be an advanced version of CookiePlus. TouchHub, a parent installer for TouchShift. TouchShift, a malware dropper capable of delivering keyloggers, screenshot utilities, and backdoors. ClientHub, a previously undocumented backdoor that comes in two versions: one that communicates with an attacker controlled server, using HTTPS and another that interacts with the Dropbox API. The end goal of the malware is to deploy additional plugins and DLLs. The plugins allow the malware to create ZIP archives, collect files matching a search pattern, delete specific files, and monitor local drive changes and return the collected status information. LPEClient, a longstanding victim profiling and payload delivery tool used since 2019. In August 2026, Check Point revealed that LPEClient was deployed following the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-68820, a privilege escalation flaw affecting Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, to deploy the FudModule rootkit. What's notable about the latest version of the malware is that it uses ML-KEM-1024, a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm, to establish an encrypted connection with the attackers' server before downloading and running additional malware directly in memory. "Operation FlashHole is the latest wave in the broader Cascade Hole campaign, which involves the use of South Korean software as a potential entry point to deliver malware targeting the country," Kaspersky said. The cybersecurity company said the emergence of Operation FlashHole coincided with a fresh wave of attacks targeting various South Korean organizations using the COPPERHEDGE backdoor. In at least one case, the backdoor infection is said to have resulted in the exfiltration of data to a dark web leak site named ULOSE, in a manner similar to Gunra ransomware attacks directed against South Korean entities around the same time. "Lazarus continues to expand its operations, launches new campaigns while introducing new tools and reworking familiar ones to meet its needs," Ryu said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "What deserves closer attention is Lazarus’s adoption of cryptography designed to withstand future quantum threats. Our findings trace its use back to at least September 2024, showing that these capabilities were already protecting the group’s malware communications more than a year before this disclosure."

fawnj9.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Malware / Cybercrime A criminal using the Amadey malware can no longer access or steal data from 180,000 infected computers around the world, including some in Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) says. The agency's operators gained access to the criminal's operation's backend and cut it off from those computers. "The next steps that we took were to disconnect that Amadey controller from all those victims," Tauri Gregory, ASD's acting deputy director-general of intelligence, told ABC News in an interview published on October 27. ASD is Australia's foreign signals intelligence and cyber security agency. Its offensive cyber operations need explicit approval from the Australian government and can disrupt cybercriminals overseas by disabling their infrastructure. Amadey was sold to criminals as a service in 2018, according to ESET's analysis of Amadey. Each buyer runs its own control panel on its own servers. Computers infected with Amadey check in with their buyer's command-and-control (C2) server and carry out its orders. Amadey's main job is to install more malware, such as the StealC infostealer. It can also steal credentials and give the buyer remote access to the machine. The most common ways Amadey reached computers were fake software updates, cracked software installers, and other malware loaders. The criminal's Amadey operation was one of many. In its tracking, ESET identified 53 separate Amadey botnets that did not share infrastructure. Disconnecting a controller from its victims also does not undo earlier theft. Credentials stolen by infostealers can sit unused for months before attackers use them, according to Microsoft's analysis. A stolen session cookie can allow an attacker to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA). ASD's annual cyber threat report, published on October 27, does not describe the operation. Amadey's infrastructure was also disrupted in June by Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement operation that works with private partners. Between June 15 and 19, the operation targeted servers associated with Amadey, StealC, and the SocGholish malware. Australia is one of nine countries whose law enforcement and judicial authorities run Operation Endgame together, according to Europol's June announcement. It was not on Europol's list of countries that took part in the June action week, and the announcement does not mention ASD. In a separate case, ASD said it received a tip that 5 terabytes of data stolen from a business were for sale. The business did not know it had been hacked. The data included business documents, personal data, and login credentials and passwords. The agency broke in and destroyed the data before it could be sold. The destroyed files included an estimated 4.8 million stolen from Australians and hundreds of thousands taken from victims in other countries.

cospwn.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Data Security OpenAI's compaction feature, which shrinks a long conversation to save space, could be turned into a way to copy a model's hidden reasoning out in plain text, security firm Xint has shown. OpenAI's reasoning models work through a problem before answering, and the service normally returns only the raw reasoning as an encrypted item the user cannot read. The method got past the protections OpenAI added in August against this kind of reasoning theft. OpenAI confirmed the problem and fixed it on October 23, according to Xint. Xint ran the technique against gpt-5.6-sol, one of OpenAI's reasoning models, using math and algorithm puzzles its researchers wrote themselves. The reasoning it pulled out came from those same requests, and Xint did not claim the method could reach another user's reasoning. Xint says it cannot prove the copied text is word-for-word the model's real reasoning, because it never had the original to compare against. Two cheaper models each repeated the item and produced the same text, which rules out mistakes in the copying step but leaves open the possibility that compaction reworded the text. Compaction is an OpenAI feature that uses a model to squeeze a long conversation into a smaller, encrypted item that carries the context forward. Xint sent a task to gpt-5.6-sol and kept the encrypted reasoning it returned. It then called the compaction step on the same model and told it to copy that reasoning into the compacted item word-for-word, with every space changed to a tab to get past OpenAI's usage-policy filters. Because compaction items can move between models, Xint passed the item to the cheaper gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o models and asked each to repeat its input exactly, which they did. The method worked around a fix OpenAI had already shipped. In August, researchers behind a paper called Stolen Thoughts showed that encrypted reasoning from a strong model could be replayed into a weaker model from the same company, which would then repeat it as plain text. OpenAI and others blocked that cross-model replay soon after. Compaction got past that block, Xint said, because the compaction step runs on the same model that made the reasoning, so it never triggers the cross-model check. The idea built on Xint's earlier work, called GhostCompact, which showed the compaction step can be pushed to run tasks of the attacker's choosing. Xint has published the code in its GitHub repository. The fix was on OpenAI's side, so developers who build on the API do not need to change anything. Xint called it an undisclosed fix and said OpenAI paid the researchers a $6,000 reward. Xint tested only gpt-5.6-sol and did not check whether GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's newer model, is affected. It is not known whether anyone used the method before OpenAI closed it. Xint also argued that fixing this one path may not be enough because, in its view, any server-side step that reads a model's decrypted reasoning and follows the user's instructions could leak it. OpenAI keeps raw reasoning hidden partly to stop distillation, where one company trains a cheaper model on another's outputs. Raw reasoning makes better training data than the final answer alone, because it shows how the model worked through the problem, which is what makes it worth stealing for a rival. OpenAI said in September that it had disrupted a July campaign that tried to expose its models' hidden reasoning, and linked a core part of it to people associated with China's Moonshot AI. Anthropic and a joint U.S. government advisory have each reported China-based labs targeting the hidden reasoning of American models. None of that is tied to Xint's compaction method, which is a demonstration rather than an attack seen in the wild.

1x3a5c0.text: The Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) has issued an alert warning of unauthorized remote access to video surveillance systems manufactured by Dahua. "Cases of compromising IP cameras and DVRs with access to the video stream, changing the device configuration and creating third-party accounts have been recorded," the State Special Communications Service of Ukraine (SSSCIP) said in an alert issued last week. The primary initial access vector used in the attacks is via Easy4IP, a peer-to-peer (P2P) platform that allows users to remotely monitor homes or small businesses by connecting their Dahua IP cameras, NVRs, and DVRs via a smartphone app or web browser by scanning a QR code or entering the hardware Serial Number (SN). The agency has warned that the serial numbers have a predictable structure containing a 10-character model prefix that's identical for all units of the same device family and a five-character hexadecimal counter that's incremented almost sequentially (e.g., 7K01F36PCA003E8). This, in turn, allows attackers to guess them at scale through a brute-force attack and identify if they are connected to the cloud without hitting rate limits or lockouts. As a result, all devices with active P2P functionality are at risk even if they cannot be accessed directly via the internet. "The assumption that the serial number is unknown to anyone is not a reason to consider the device secure," CERT-UA said. Authentication barriers are overcome by leveraging weak or known passwords, or by exploiting authentication bypass vulnerabilities in outdated firmware versions, such as CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045. CERT-UA has shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the activity - Presence of unknown accounts Unauthorized configuration changes Audit logs containing authentication events using the manufacturer's native protocol (DVRIP) and from a local address (127.0.0.1), a sign of P2P access. To counter the threat, it's advised to disable the P2P feature if not required, avoid exposing them directly to the internet, and keep the software up-to-date. The agency has not disclosed who was targeted, when these infections occurred, how many devices had been infected, or who was responsible for the activity. However, the findings share similarities with two clusters of activity that Hunt.io disclosed as targeting IP cameras in Ukraine and Russia. One of the campaigns, attributed to a Russian-speaking operator, singled out internet-exposed cameras in Ukraine using known Dahua and Hikvision vulnerabilities, ultimately compromising 58 devices. The activity involved the exploitation of the following flaws by integrating Ingram, a publicly available webcam vulnerability scanner - CVE-2017-7921 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Hikvision CVE-2020-25078 - A credential disclosure vulnerability in D-Link CVE-2020-25169 - An unauthenticated information disclosure vulnerability in Reolink CVE-2021-33044 / CVE-2021-33045 - Authentication bypass vulnerabilities in Dahua that allow passwordless login CVE-2021-36260 - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Hikvision. In parallel, the threat actor is also said to have undertaken scanning and exploitation of TP-Link and MikroTik routers and cameras using vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-53375 and CVE-2024-57049 across 15 European countries, including Ukraine, Poland, Romania, Moldova, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, the U.K., and Austria. The second campaign, codenamed Operation CameraSwarm and attributed to a lone threat actor, is believed to have compromised over 14,530 Dahua IP cameras between June 17 and July 22, 2026, using a combination of credential brute-force attacks and the exploitation of the CVE-2021-33044-CVE-2021-33045 chain. The attack scans for TCP port 37777, which is the default proprietary management and video streaming port used by Dahua, followed by collecting serial numbers, breaking into those devices by employing the aforementioned two exploitation methods, and then deploying a persistent backdoor account ("p2pwn / p2password") on nearly 2,000 cameras in a manner that can survive password change and a factory reset. "1,923 cameras carry a persistent backdoor account (p2pwn / p2password), installed over RPC after either bypass," Hunt.io noted at the time. "It is stored independently of the admin password and survives a password change and, on most firmware, a factory reset. 283 cameras were reached by serial number alone through Dahua's cloud relay, with no device address and, in most cases, no credentials." In some instances, the attackers have been found to abuse Dahua's cloud relay to reach cameras behind NATs using only their serial numbers. Earlier this year, Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian actors are compromising IP cameras across the E.U., NATO states, and Ukraine to conduct systematic digital espionage operations and acquire military intelligence. "This actor performs automated analysis of imagery through image recognition software to conduct targeted searches for military vehicles and the military cargo they are transporting," the July 2026 bulletin said. "This provides the actor with, among other things, relevant military data, such as E.U. and NATO military transport routes, weapon deliveries to Ukraine, and the locations of Ukrainian military personnel. The information from IP cameras in Ukraine is used in attempts to neutralize Ukrainian military personnel and to destroy their military material."

9gjiyy.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 27, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday confirmed active exploitation of the recently patched PHP2Shell flaws by adding them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The PHP vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scoring system, facilitate unauthenticated remote code execution on affected deployments - CVE-2026-109618 - An out-of-memory corruption vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109619 - A stale internal request-state vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution. The addition of the two flaws to the KEV catalog comes after Adel Karimi, detection and response lead at Perplexity, confirmed successful instances of remote code execution against honeypot systems on October 24, 2026. "This is now confirmed RCE with usable memory disclosure, not just a crash followed by a suspicious process," Karimi said. "The response delivered an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, and a function address derived from that dump using the public exploit's offsets appears in the subsequent execution payload." "The evidence demonstrates this chain on the intentionally favorable single-worker mod_php profile; it is not a measurement of exploit reliability on other worker counts, PHP builds, or applications." The issues have been addressed in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 released on October 21, 2026. Federal agencies have time until October 29, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes. PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is a server-side scripting language used in roughly 70% of all websites on the internet. According to estimates shared by Censys, more than 32.51 million PHP services are still running an affected version. The severity of the vulnerabilities has prompted numerous advisories from software and security vendors and government agencies across the world, including - ABB Arista Networks Belden Broadcom Canon Citrix Craft CMS Dell Dormakaba Drupal ExpressionEngine F5 Hikvision HP HPE Hitachi Energy HMS Networks Huawei IBM Ivanti Johnson Controls Mitel Moxa NETGEAR October CMS Okta QNAP Rockwell Automation Ruckus Wireless Salesforce Schneider Electric Siemens (1), (2) SonicWall Splunk Synology Veeam Wibu-Systems WordPress As of October 26, 2026, the PHP Foundation also released Windows builds 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1 to address CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder library that could also result in privilege escalation and unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerability, also known as Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell, affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0. It has been patched in versions 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1, along with other projects that include the C library, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, and Python. "In PHP Windows builds, the vulnerable decoder can be reached through the cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is enabled," the PHP Foundation said. "This is disabled by default in cURL, but applications and HTTP client libraries can enable it."

e9bla9.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 26, 2026Malware / Web Security An unknown threat actor has infected 953 online stores, most of them running Magento, as part of a long-running campaign active since July 2025. According to Dutch e-commerce security company Sansec, the activity is designed to add a small piece of code to the store's pages that, when visited by unsuspecting users, serves malicious JavaScript loader code through Magento CMS blocks. "When you visit, that code makes your browser ask the group's server what to do next," Sansec said. "The server first checks whether you are a real shopper or a security scanner, so scanners get nothing." No less than five distinct domains have been observed over time in connection with the campaign - manulfie[.]click, first seen in July 2025 neswnsssn[.]click, first seen in December 2025 lanhd6549tdhse[.]top, first seen in March 2026 additionalver[.]com, first seen in June 2026 deepveindrilling[.]com, first seen in October 2026 Sansec said it found deepveindrilling[.]com in the CMS blocks of 83 online stores since the domain was registered on October 6, 2026. The latest JavaScript loader domain is hosted behind Cloudflare and only responds to script requests from real visitors of infected stores. The loader is staged within Magento's cms_block database table, which is used to render static content into storefront pages. The ultimate objective of the attack is to launch the attack-controlled code when the CMS block is rendered after a shopper opens the compromised website. While Sansec does not disclose whether the threat actor modifies an existing CMS block (such as header, footer, or promotional banner) or creates a new block, the attacker can adopt either of the approaches to run the loader. Two different versions of the loader have been spotted. In one version, the external JavaScript loaded from the attacker's domain stores the payload in the browser's localStorage. This causes the stashed code to be run again on subsequent visits, even if the external domain becomes unavailable. The second version expands on this behavior by incorporating browser fingerprinting checks to filter out bots and security scanners, while ensuring that only real shoppers are exposed to the malicious code. The exact nature of the final payload remains unknown. Early iterations of the campaign have also been observed using Keitaro, an advertising tracker and analytics platform, as a traffic distribution system (TDS), to route visitors to different responses – i.e., return a payload, a redirect or nothing – based on their characteristics. Sansec said requesting the additionalver[.]com script as a Windows desktop visitor returned as response "QWE=123;," which does nothing apart from setting a cookie that marks the visitor for 24 hours. The deepveindrilling[.]com domain, on the other hand, drops the Keitaro component and integrates the bot-filtering logic into the loader itself. As for the initial access vector, 471 Magento stores are estimated to have been injected with the loader through the PolyShell (aka CVE-2026-48356) vulnerability. Another 102 stores saw files uploaded through the PolyShell or SessionReaper (aka CVE-2025-54236) vulnerabilities. "One store on Magento 2.4.7-p1 had PolyShell webshells disguised as PNG images in pub/media/custom_options/quote/, next to the additionalver.com loader in a CMS block," Sansec said. "The block switched to deepveindrilling[.]com on October 7. The store still lacks APSB26-73, Adobe's PolyShell fix for supported release lines." In another case, an e-commerce store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 with no missing core patches was compromised to add a rogue administrator account and then use it to inject the code. Site owners are advised to audit their sites for suspicious accounts and unexpected CMS blocks in the cms_block and cms_page tables. It's also advised to keep the sites up-to-date and enforce strong passwords. The disclosure comes against the backdrop of PHP2Shell, a set of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that have witnessed widespread exploitation attempts following their disclosure last week. However, Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi has recorded what appears to be the first in-the-wild successful exploitation of the vulnerabilities to run shell commands on honeypot servers. These commands have been observed using wget, curl, or PHP CLI to fetch additional payloads from a remote server ("162.35.99[.]94:80").No downloaded second-stage artifacts have been observed so far.

1s77uzf.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code. PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on. The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws. They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1, the fixed version. PHP publishes a software bill of materials, a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions. PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page. Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip, and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build. Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports. Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system. An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts. Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1, or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale. Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update. Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21. Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes. PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it." In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING, because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false, which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed.

15myic.text: Cybersecurity researchers are calling attention to what they say is a "recurring social engineering pattern" across hundreds of cases in which threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation feature to conduct impersonation scams or to deliver malware. "A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The attacks consistently employ IT-themed display names or friendly-sounding first names to subvert external-user warnings in Teams. These messages originate from Teams identities established through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Nearly 30–40% of the cases investigated by the cybersecurity company involve the use of *.onmicrosoft[.]com, a permanent fallback domain automatically generated by Microsoft when a Microsoft 365 tenant is created. These domains masquerade as IT infrastructure, opting for a help desk- or support-themed word as the tenant name to increase their credibility - helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft[.]com itendpoint365.onmicrosoft[.]com itcoreportal.onmicrosoft[.]com itadmin922.onmicrosoft[.]com corporateitservicellc.onmicrosoft[.]com As observed in many cases before, these Teams sessions are preceded by mail bombing, where the victim's inbox is flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations in a short span of time. The approach is designed to induce a false sense of urgency, with the Teams IT support message arriving soon after to help resolve the problem. Some of the display names observed by Arctic Wolf across different cases are listed below - Help Desk IT Support HelpDesk Manager IT Service Desk – Liam / IT Service Desk (Liam) IT Service Desk – Matt / IT Service Desk – Scott IT Support – Christopher Thomas HelpDesk Supervisor Enterprise IT & Security (Internal) IT Tech Support Internal Business IT Solutions & Support (Internal) Maintenance Service IT-Representative IT/Help Desk In recent iterations, the attackers have been observed adding the target organization's domain or company name in their display name to lend the messages additional legitimacy. "We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation," Arctic Wolf said. "Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br." The activity aligns with that of STAC4749, has a history of creating IT-themed cloud domains under the ".top" TLD and leveraging plausible employee usernames to make the accounts appear authentic. These attacks have led to the deployment of Chaos ransomware, according to Sophos. The attacks specifically go after organizations where external access is enabled. This also involves an element of vishing to trick victims to granting them hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool like Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn. The remote access is abused to conduct reconnaissance, deliver additional payloads like the GoGRPC backdoor, facilitate lateral movement to domain controllers, and deploy additional RMM tools like Level for redundancy, before exfiltrating sensitive data and dropping the ransomware binary. "In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft's notes," Arctic Wolf said. "Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.' In one case identified by the cybersecurity vendor, the threat actor is said to have instructed the user to run a PowerShell command to download a file and then launch it. The PowerShell command is designed to download an MSI installer from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. When the victim runs the installer, it launches a PowerShell script responsible for extracting and executing a Python implant embedded within it. The backdoor then runs another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects and then transmits the information to an external server. "External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability," Arctic Wolf said. "Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise."

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. oapp2e.text: Anthropic has introduced OSS Scanner, a free service that checks critical open-source repositories for security vulnerabilities and sends findings directly to project maintainers. The opt-in program uses the company’s strongest AI models to run repeated scans, giving developers a faster route to potential flaws without waiting for human review. According to Anthropic’s service overview, OSS Scanner builds on its work with Project Glasswing. The company says it had reviewed more than 6,000 vulnerability reports by October 2026 through its existing disclosure process. The new service offers a separate path for projects willing to assess AI-generated reports. Anthropic OSS Scanner According to the GitHub repository, the scanner first builds an enrolled project inside an isolated virtual machine with network access enabled. This stage installs dependencies and prepares the software for testing. Anthropic then removes Internet access before the security audit begins, allowing scanning agents to examine the project within a restricted environment. Reports arrive by email with steps to reproduce the suspected issue and a proposed patch where available. Anthropic says its pipeline includes agents that double-check bugs and examine their root causes. However, these checks are automated. A human does not review the findings before maintainers receive them. After the first scan, the service checks projects again for newly introduced vulnerabilities and issues missed earlier. Scan frequency depends on factors such as demand and project usage. This extends Anthropic’s wider push into security research, including earlier work in which Claude uncovered 22 Firefox vulnerabilities. Core maintainers apply through the official GitHub repository by opening a pull request that adds a directory under projects/<name>. Each submission needs a project.yaml configuration containing the repository address and a primary contact email. Anthropic manually checks that applicants are core maintainers before accepting a project. Eligibility focuses on established projects with broad use, exposure to remote attacks, and significant infrastructure security impact. A Dockerfile must explain how to install dependencies and build the software. Developers can keep it in their own repository or beside project.yaml in the enrollment repository. Everything needed for building and testing must be downloaded during setup because the later audit cannot access the Internet. An optional threat_model.md file helps guide the scan. Maintainers can describe where untrusted input enters, which components are outside scope, and how they rate severity. They can also explain preferred report formats and patch requirements, reducing the need for the scanner to guess project-specific security expectations. Before applying, developers can use tools/validate.py to check their configuration and tools/check <name> to test the build. The checking tool runs with network access, so Anthropic warns users to test only trusted projects or use a separate machine. Configuration email addresses are public, making a dedicated security alias useful. Maintainers can add an OpenPGP public key for encrypted reports, but encrypted messages go only to the primary contact and cannot include additional recipients. Anthropic does not impose a 90-day disclosure deadline on unvalidated findings. However, a report later confirmed through its human-reviewed program may enter that disclosure process. This safeguard matters amid concerns about AI-generated vulnerability reports wasting maintainers’ time. Project owners still need to reproduce suspected flaws and test suggested fixes before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities. Reports can be paused with disabled: true, while deleting the enrollment directory withdraws the project entirely Cut every SOC alert investigation by 21 min. 1u9k9io.text: Let’s Encrypt will cut its default TLS certificate lifetime from 90 days to 64 days on February 10, 2027, giving website operators less time between renewals. The change applies to certificates issued or renewed from that date, while subscribers can still choose shorter certificate profiles offering 45 days or roughly six days. Let’s Encrypt Certificate Lifetime According to the October 7 announcement published by Let’s Encrypt, the nonprofit certificate authority confirmed the schedule. Existing certificates will remain valid until their normal expiry dates, and Let’s Encrypt will not revoke them as part of the transition. It expects the final 90-day certificate to expire on May 11, 2027. The shorter lifetime limits how long a certificate can remain trusted after a private key is stolen or a certificate is issued incorrectly. It also makes reliable renewal systems more important, especially for teams still using fixed schedules or manual steps. The move is part of the wider shift toward shorter public TLS certificate lifetimes. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CA/Browser Forum’s plan to reduce maximum validity to 47 days. Let’s Encrypt is moving faster, with its default profile set to 45 days on February 16, 2028, as outlined in its earlier certificate lifetime roadmap. Let’s Encrypt will start issuing 64-day certificates in its staging environment on October 14, 2026. Administrators can use this test service to check renewal behavior before the production change. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers and should not replace certificates on live websites. For automated setups, the key feature is ACME Renewal Information, or ARI. ACME is the protocol used to request and renew certificates automatically. ARI lets Let’s Encrypt tell a supported client when to renew, helping it adjust to shorter lifetimes without relying on a fixed calendar. Administrators should check their client’s documentation to confirm ARI support. When ARI isn’t available, Let’s Encrypt recommends renewing at about two-thirds of the certificate’s lifetime. For a 64-day certificate, that means around day 43, rather than waiting until the old 60-day renewal point. The authority also recommends searching cron jobs, wrapper scripts, and runbooks for hardcoded values such as 83, 80, or 60. These numbers may reveal renewal rules designed around 90-day certificates. Updating those rules now also prepares systems for the 45-day default planned for 2028. Alongside certificate validity, Let’s Encrypt will reduce authorization reuse from 30 days to 10 days. This is the period during which an earlier domain control check can support another certificate request without repeating that check. The reuse period will fall to seven hours in 2028. Let’s Encrypt says this supports upcoming validation rules and removes the need for separate Certificate Authority Authorization rechecks on older validation data. Most subscribers will not need changes unless their ACME setup specifically depends on authorization reuse. Rate limits will not change because of the shorter lifetimes, according to Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit guidance. ACME endpoints and certificate issuance chains will also remain unchanged. Operators should test the full certificate workflow, including deployment and service reloads, rather than checking renewal alone. Teams managing many websites should also confirm that renewed certificates reach every server and that monitoring checks the certificate actually served to users after each reload. Alerts for failed renewals can help teams catch problems before expiry. The practical priority is dependable automation that keeps certificates current as renewal windows shrink. j5jng0.text: Microsoft is urging organizations to prepare their certificate systems for post-quantum authentication, warning that public key infrastructure (PKI), hardware security modules (HSMs), and security appliances need testing before deployment. Its October 8 guidance says the shift will affect applications, devices, certificate chains, and the processes that keep digital trust working. The message goes beyond protecting encrypted traffic. While many quantum security plans focus on attackers collecting data now to decrypt later, authentication depends on certificates and private keys being issued, stored, checked, renewed, and managed across different vendors. Changing the underlying algorithms can expose gaps across that entire chain. Microsoft Security Researchs noted that organizations often know where TLS protects communications but lack a complete view of certificate dependencies. Their report concerns infrastructure readiness, not a newly discovered malware campaign. Post-Quantum Authentication The main challenge is not simply finding a quantum-resistant algorithm. Businesses must establish whether their existing systems can use new certificates reliably. Older PKI deployments, embedded devices, operational technology, custom applications, and third-party services may contain fixed assumptions that only become visible during testing. Larger post-quantum certificates and certificate chains can affect connection setup, storage, transmission, and network inspection limits. Related work on Cloudflare’s post-quantum certificate authority shows why certificate size and connection speed matter as providers explore different designs for quantum-safe authentication. Those efforts do not remove the need to test enterprise systems individually. HSM providers and security appliance vendors therefore belong in the migration discussion from the start. Teams need to check whether hardware-backed systems support future certificate requirements and whether monitoring, inspection, and certificate-management tools can process the resulting traffic. Support in one application does not establish readiness across the full environment. Microsoft’s PQC TLS Pilot Microsoft launched its Post-Quantum Cryptography TLS Pilot Program on August 27, 2026. It allows approved certificate authorities in good standing with the Microsoft Trusted Root Program to test certificate roots and issuance using ML-DSA-87, a quantum-resistant digital signature algorithm. The focus is compatibility, performance, and day-to-day operations. The August release added seven pilot roots operated by ComSign, DigiCert, HARICA, IdenTrust Services, Sectigo, Shanghai Electronic Certification Authority, and SSL.com. Admissions continue through the end of 2026. Microsoft’s published authentication readiness guidance directs eligible providers to the Trusted Root Program portal for requirements and applications. These certificates are not publicly trusted. Microsoft limits their use to closed environments, custom applications, and enterprise testbeds, explicitly excluding production trust and public-facing websites. Elsewhere, Let’s Encrypt’s certificate roadmap explores Merkle Tree Certificates for public-web authentication, highlighting that separate efforts are addressing different parts of the transition. On supported, correctly configured Windows 11 systems, pilot testing begins with the July 28, 2026 updates. Microsoft names KB5101681, OS Build 28000.2608, for 26H1, and KB5101684, OS Builds 26200.8973 and 26100.8973, for 25H2. ML-DSA certificates can also work with Secure Channel, or Schannel, in supported scenarios. Administrators must confirm platform requirements before testing. Software and hardware readiness should be checked separately. Earlier coverage of Google’s quantum-safe digital signatures described software-based Cloud KMS support with hardware-backed support planned separately. Microsoft similarly urges organizations to ask certificate providers, HSM vendors, software suppliers, and platform vendors about their roadmaps and testing capabilities rather than assume universal support. Security teams should inventory certificate-dependent systems, map public and private trust relationships, and identify equipment with long upgrade cycles. Non-production tests should cover compatibility, performance, and operational workflows. Developments such as OpenSSL’s post-quantum performance improvements offer useful testing context, but preview software and Microsoft’s pilot certificates should not be treated as production-ready replacements. That work should include the full certificate lifecycle, not just a successful connection. Issuance, distribution, validation, renewal, and management all depend on linked systems. Testing those steps together helps teams find process gaps that a standalone algorithm test could miss before they reach live business services. Microsoft recommends a multi-year program with named owners, clear dependencies, and modernization priorities based on test results. Organizations can ask their certificate provider whether it participates in the pilot and offers suitable testing. The practical goal is to uncover failures before quantum-resistant authentication becomes a large-scale deployment requirement. 6tjopr.text: VirusTotal has added daily scanning of the public IPv4 space, giving security teams a new way to find command-and-control (C2) servers and track malware infrastructure. Announced on October 8, 2026, the update records exposed services, port activity, banners, and server fingerprints alongside existing threat intelligence. The change helps researchers look beyond an IP address’s detection score. Earlier reports showed hosting details, passive DNS records, and files that contacted an address. The new data shows what a server exposes now, helping analysts find related hosts that have no malware detections. A new Ports tab lists open, closed, and recently closed ports, together with service names, software versions, and timestamps. Records also include SSH host keys, RDP fingerprints, HTTP headers, and operating system details inferred from service responses. VirusTotal keeps records when ports stop responding. Researchers can therefore check when a suspected C2 service was last seen online and compare that date with changes elsewhere in a campaign. This history adds context that a current detection score cannot provide. VirusTotal Adds Daily Internet Scanning The official announcement describes searches through the web interface and API. Queries such as entity:ip open_port:22 find exposed SSH services. Bracket syntax ties conditions to specific ports, preventing a product on one port from being incorrectly matched with a version on another. These searches build on the methods covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal threat research guide. One investigation started with 91.219.237[.]110, an address listed in APT28 and Havoc collections. Its SSH fingerprint led researchers to 185.146.232[.]3, which had no detections, collections, or communicating files. Both hosts shared an OpenSSH build, nginx configuration, and an unusual certificate name, b4ck.my. Searching that certificate name uncovered a third address, 96.9.125[.]59. Port timestamps suggested one server was being retired around the time another appeared. However, VirusTotal warned that older malware links do not establish current ownership or APT28 attribution because IP addresses can change hands. Fingerprint matches also need careful checks. Some SSH keys appeared across more than 1,400 cloud addresses because server templates reused them. An open port alone is similarly weak evidence. Searching Cobalt Strike’s default team server port returned over 1.5 million addresses, including hosts answering on many ports. Another example exposed a NOX Stealer login panel at 5.175.221[.]206 on port 8443. The host also exposed SMB and RDP, with scan data identifying Windows Server 2022, nginx 1.24.0, and PHP 8.3.33. Combining those traits reduced a search from 4.5 million hosts to ten candidates, not ten confirmed malicious servers. When the panel changed its name to BOMBAY Stealer, browser analysis captured the new title while the exposed services stayed unchanged. Researchers also searched FTP banners containing “conhost,” finding five addresses tied to command-delivery patterns discussed in E4del and PINHOLE research. Port data is available through API records and history endpoints, but not yet through IP Livehunt rules. Saved searches run on a schedule offer a workaround. Teams planning automation can consult Cybersecuritynews.com’s VirusTotal access overview and API documentation and check their account limits. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. fow618.text: Alleged internal chats from Silent Ransom Group suggest the criminals collected $206.95 million from 27 firms in roughly six months without encrypting victims’ files. The reported earnings point to the power of data extortion, where attackers steal sensitive records and demand payment to keep them private. However, the payment figures remain unverified, and the group denies breaching its systems or leaking its chats. DataBreaches reported the alleged leak on October 7. The material contains 5,692 messages covering August 27, 2025, through September 29, 2026. Discussions reportedly include victim negotiations, payments, access methods, and members’ spending. An October 8 update said Silent Ransom Group had agreed to an interview but disputed the leak’s origin. Silent Ransomware Extorted Over $200,000,000 The chats mark completed deals as “GOLD.” Adding those entries produces the $206.95 million total. Crystal Intelligence dates the 27 claimed payments between April 3 and September 24, 2026, placing the reported earnings within a period of less than six months. These entries reflect the criminals’ own records, not audited financial results. According to DataBreaches, the median alleged payment was $6 million, while individual amounts ranged from $100,000 to $30 million. White & Case was listed against the largest amount. Nine named firms disclosed breaches relevant to the period. However, those disclosures do not confirm who attacked them or whether they paid the sums shown. Crystal Intelligence’s blockchain analysis found transactions matching the timing of several chat entries. One upstream collection wallet received about 344 bitcoin, valued at roughly $27 million, over six weeks. Researchers could not connect individual victim payments to that wallet. Hence, the evidence supports substantial money movement rather than proving the headline total. 1w6ljoy.text: A malicious Android PDF reader distributed through Google Play has recorded more than 10,000 installs while serving as an installer for the Anatsa banking trojan. The finding shows how a routine document tool can become a route for malware that puts banking passwords and financial accounts at risk. The installation figure describes the reach of the reader app, not a confirmed count of successful banking infections or stolen accounts. The available alert also does not identify affected banks, victim countries, financial losses, or whether Google has since removed this particular listing, wile those details remain unconfirmed. Researchers from Zscaler ThreatLabz identified the malicious installer and shared its indicators in an October 8 alert on X. They described the application as an Android PDF reader with over 10,000 installs and published separate file hashes for the installer and the Anatsa payload, alongside their command-and-control addresses. The discovery follows earlier cases involving similar disguises. In April, a fake document reader campaign used a different package to distribute Anatsa before Google removed that app. That earlier removal should not be confused with the status of the newly reported reader, which the current alert does not establish. Malicious PDF Reader With 10,000+ Installs Anatsa, also known as TeaBot, uses a dropper model: the app installed first acts as a delivery tool for a separate malicious component. This separation helps explain why a download that appears useful can later expose a phone to banking malware. The latest alert identifies both stages but does not provide a full execution trace. In its technical analysis of Anatsa, ThreatLabz documented earlier campaigns that downloaded additional code and presented the final payload as an app update. Some samples checked the device environment before proceeding, helping the malware avoid test systems used by researchers. These are documented family techniques, not confirmed findings for every new sample. ThreatLabz also documented malformed APK archive headers that made older payloads harder to inspect, along with encrypted code loaded at runtime. APK files are Android installation packages; hiding their contents can disrupt tools that inspect files without running them. The new alert does not confirm whether these samples use those methods. The broader use of Google Play stealth loaders shows why unexpected update requests deserve attention even when the original app came from an official store. A request to install an extra component outside the normal update process can move the user from a harmless-looking utility to the banking payload. ThreatLabz has uncovered another new Anatsa installer that is distributed via the Google Play Store. The application is disguised as an Android PDF reader that currently has over 10,000 installs. The IOCs for this campaign are listed below: Google Play Store URL… pic.twitter.com/duQA0myTAi — Zscaler ThreatLabz (@Threatlabz) October 8, 2026 For this campaign, ThreatLabz listed one installer-related command-and-control URL and two payload command-and-control endpoints. Keeping those roles separate matters during an investigation: the installer and the banking trojan are different files, and each has its own published MD5 hash. The alert does not explain the exact contents returned by the installer URL. Why Banking Accounts Are at Risk Earlier ThreatLabz research found that Anatsa requested SMS and accessibility permissions, contacted its control server, and checked for targeted financial apps. The server then supplied fake login pages matching apps on the phone. Credentials entered into those pages were sent to the attackers rather than the bank. A previous Anatsa document reader outbreak reached more than 100,000 downloads and used fake banking screens to capture account details. That history explains the concern around this new reader, but its target list and permission behavior still require sample-specific verification rather than assumptions based on older campaigns. What Android Users Should Do Users who installed the identified reader should remove it, review granted permissions, and scan their phones with a trusted security tool. Keep Google Play Protect enabled and question unexpected requests for SMS or accessibility access. If banking activity looks suspicious, contact the bank promptly and change account passwords from a trusted device. For security teams, the package name can support app inventory checks, while file hashes help match samples against the reported installer and payload. Network logs can be searched for the listed domain and IP endpoints. Matches should be reviewed in context to establish which device communicated, when contact occurred, and whether malware executed. 7ebrhx.text: A prolific hacker with the Syrian Electronic Army was sentenced to more than three years in prison for carrying out cyber campaigns against nearly 50 Western targets, the Justice Department announced this week. Ahmad Umar Agha, known online as “Th3Pr0,” was sentenced Thursday in federal court in Virginia to 42 months behind bars for his role in a conspiracy that was organized by former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's closest advisers. The hacking group has been involved since at least 2011 in computer intrusions in support of Assad, whose government was eventually overthrown by a rebel coalition in 2024 after a protracted civil war. In one notable 2013 incident, the group said it hijacked the Associated Press’s Twitter account and sent out a tweet that falsely reported an explosion at the White House had injured President Barack Obama. The hoax caused a brief $136 billion dip in the stock market. A 2014 FBI affidavit said that Twitter's message confirming a password reset for the account was sent to an email address used by Agha. In another attack, Agha gained access to a company hosting the Marine Corps’ recruiting website and redirected visitors to a propaganda message that urged service members to disobey orders and join the Syrian Army. The U.S. first charged Agha for his criminal activities in 2014. In 2016, the FBI added him and another member of the Syrian Electronic Army, Firas Dardar, to its Cyber's Most Wanted list with a $100,000 reward. Both men were indicted by a federal grand jury in 2018. Agha was taken into U.S. custody last year, however the DOJ has not given details of his arrest. Dardar remains a fugitive. All together, Agha hacked about 47 Western media outlets, non-profit groups and other entities allied with the U.S., according to the DOJ. The department also said the group’s digital conspiracy collected intelligence for Assad’s government before its fall. "Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad's regime to silence reporting on the regime's atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders," John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in a statement. labqfn.text: A malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code VS Code extension was distributed through Cursor's extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29, exposing up to 5,000 developers to malware designed to install persistent SSH backdoors. The extension used the version number 2.1.313 and was distributed between 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. Pacific Time. Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built from Microsoft’s open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), with support for VS Code extensions. Anthropic’s Claude Code extension brings its AI coding assistant directly into compatible editors, helping developers write and debug code using natural-language instructions. Cursor says Anthropic did not develop the malicious extension but has not explained how attackers distributed the compromised package under Anthropic's name. "Between about 2:27 am PT and 1:35 pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code extension Marketplace," warned Cursor. "The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor." Researchers at Phorion and OpenSourceMalware found that the attackers inserted a malicious JavaScript loader at the beginning of the extension's extension.js file, leaving the legitimate extension code otherwise unchanged. The malicious code executes when the extension loads, without requiring user interaction with Claude Code. When installed, the malicious extension performs the following actions on compromised systems: Collects system and user information, including Git email and public IP address. Adds an attacker-controlled SSH key and attempts to enable SSH access and establish a reverse tunnel. Installs persistence through a macOS LaunchAgent or Windows scheduled task/Startup script, retrying the tunnel roughly every minute. Sends host details and backdoor status to the attacker’s server at the IP address 134.209.82[.]225 Attack chain Source: OpenSourceMalware However, according to Phorion, coding errors in the malware's SSH setup routines likely prevented attackers from gaining remote access to many affected Windows and macOS systems. The mistakes prevented the malware from enabling SSH on machines where it was not already running, leaving the reverse tunnel unable to provide access to the compromised device. On macOS, the malware attempts to check whether Remote Login is enabled using the systemsetup -getremotelogin command, but runs it without elevated privileges. Instead of returning the SSH service's status, the command produces an administrator-access error. Because the malware only attempts to enable SSH when the output contains "Off," it skips the activation step entirely. On Windows, the malware attempts to install and start the OpenSSH server through PowerShell, but it tries to do so via /bin/sh, a Unix shell that isn't available on standard Windows installations. Due to this, the SSH setup fails. In both cases, the malware can still install its SSH keys, establish persistence, and attempt to create the reverse tunnel. However, if the SSH server is not already running, the tunnel cannot provide access to the compromised machine. Even if the SSH backdoor fails, the malware still sends reconnaissance data to the attacker's server, including the victim's username, hostname, public IP address, Git email address, and names of environment variables associated with sensitive credentials. However, the script does not directly steal credentials, suggesting the attackers intended to retrieve sensitive data manually after gaining access through the SSH tunnel. Cursor removed the malicious extension and temporarily shut down its entire marketplace to audit other extensions and rotate all access keys before making it available again. The company also worked with the hosting provider to take the attacker's server offline, disrupting both the reverse SSH connections and the transmission of reconnaissance data. Following an internal investigation, Cursor says it found no evidence that any other extension versions or the official distribution were affected. Those who have downloaded the package during the exposure window should check for the presence of an 'svc-telemetry' SSH key on their machines, and follow Cursor’s remediation instructions if impact is confirmed. For impacted machines, it is recommended to isolate them, rotate accessible secrets, invalidate sessions, and rebuild the affected environment from safe backups. While initial reports suggested that npm, Open VSX, and Microsoft's Visual Studio Code Marketplace were also impacted, it was later confirmed that Cursor was the only source distributing the malicious extension. However, many questions remain unanswered about the supply chain attack, including how the threat actors published a malicious extension under Anthropic's name on Cursor's marketplace and whether Cursor or Anthropic's systems were compromised during the incident. BleepingComputer contacted Anthropic and Cursor with questions about the attack and will update this story if we receive a response.
