xvj9jh.text: British cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ cannot account for thousands of “USB sticks, external hard drives, compact discs, memory cards and other portable media storage devices,” the official watchdog has disclosed. The Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office (IPCO) in its annual report for 2025, published Thursday, said it was “very concerned” and “disappointed with the time it has taken GCHQ to investigate” the issue. The commissioner, Sir Brian Leveson, said GCHQ had “not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location and recoverability” of the lost devices, and said the underlying issues had been raised several years ago. The report describes removable media as “utilised extensively” by the agency and an essential component of some of its operating processes. GCHQ estimated the total losses as “in the thousands.” Some of the devices may contain data obtained under the Investigatory Powers Act, including powers allowing spies and police to intercept communications and hack suspect devices. The report does not allege that any of the devices have fallen into the hands of adversaries. A spokesperson for GCHQ declined to answer whether it was aware of unauthorised persons accessing any of the missing media. They said the agency acknowledged its “management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use.” Framing the issue as a record-keeping problem, rather than one of lost items, the spokesperson said IPCO was “right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations.” “We recognise the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items,” they added. “The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken.” It is understood GCHQ has since conducted a full audit of the items it holds and updated its processes and tools, and has kept IPCO informed of its progress. It is unclear whether the audit has established how many items are lost. Errorism IPCO’s report also reveals that flawed GCHQ intelligence misidentified selectors — identifiers such as phone numbers or online accounts — in “a small number of cases” where innocent members of the public were “wrongly suspected of being involved in terrorism-related criminality.” The misidentifications led to actions against members of the public, including five stops at ports (potentially including airports and international train terminals) under counter-terrorism powers. At these stops, people were detained, had their devices downloaded and biometrics taken. According to the report, the misidentifications occurred because of “a particular software application” which was not named. It was described as “one of a class of internet applications used by a relatively small section of the public. However, this particular application operated in an unusual way which meant, unbeknownst to GCHQ, that the target discovery methodology was unreliable.” Target discovery is the process of identifying previously unknown people who may be of intelligence interest, typically using communications data. The report did not explain how the app frustrated this process. The possibilities include a range of technologies that route traffic through other users’ devices that could make innocent people appear to be in contact with a suspect. IPCO said GCHQ could not have foreseen the issue. It added “although the impact on those affected is highly unfortunate and regrettable, intelligence can sometimes simply be wrong.” The agency “acted to minimise the effects of these misidentifications as soon as it became aware of the issue,” said IPCO. GCHQ’s spokesperson declined to comment on the target discovery issue. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. 1s9pd7a.text: Attackers have started exploiting a maximum-severity GitLab vulnerability patched earlier this month, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Tracked as CVE-2026-97229, this critical security flaw was discovered by a security researcher using the 'joaxcar' handle in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, which parses, compiles, and evaluates regular expressions in pipeline configuration files. CVE-2026-97229 stems from an integer overflow weakness and could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances via a maliciously crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient expression validation. "GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server via a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration, due to insufficient regular expression validation," it said. GitLab addressed the security issue in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 and urged admins to patch their servers immediately. The company has also released threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances after detecting exploitation attempts. On Thursday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed active exploitation and added CVE-2026-97229 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog. CISA also ordered federal agencies to secure their servers by Sunday, as mandated by Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. Although BOD 26-04 targets only federal agencies, the cybersecurity agency encouraged all security teams, including those in the private sector, to prioritize patching this flaw to protect their networks against ongoing attacks. Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver tracks nearly 2,800 Internet-exposed GitLab Community Edition instances, but it doesn't say how many have already been secured against attacks. GitLab CE instances exposed online (Shadowserver) ​CVE-2026-97229 is the latest in a string of security issues GitLab has addressed since the start of the year. In January, it patched a high-severity two-factor authentication bypass (CVE-2026-0723) that lets attackers who know the target's account ID circumvent two-factor authentication. Earlier this month, it also fixed a maximum-severity Regular Expression Compiler flaw (CVE-2026-110264) that could let remote attackers run arbitrary code on targeted instances. Almost two weeks later, GitLab addressed another maximum-severity vulnerability (CVE-2026-85706) in the repository commits API that can be abused to read sensitive data, such as credentials and other secrets, from vulnerable servers. One day later, CISA added CVE-2026-85706 to its list of actively exploited flaws after cybersecurity firm watchTowr reported that attackers had already begun scanning the Internet for unpatched GitLab servers. CISA has tagged six GitLab vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, including two (tracked as CVE-2021-22175 and CVE-2021-39935) in February this year. GitLab's DevSecOps platform is used by over 50% of Fortune 100 companies and has more than 70 million registered users worldwide. 3tky5x.text: SS7 and Diameter signaling attacks can track, intercept, and impersonate you. Here’s how they work and how to stop them. Your phone can be tracked, your SMS two-factor codes can be intercepted, and your number can be impersonated, all without malware, a phishing link, or any access to your device. The attacks happen inside the telecom network, in the carrier-to-carrier control protocols known as signaling, the automated descendants of the old telephone switchboard. Most users never see them, and most carriers can’t reliably stop them. Signaling attacks aren’t new. Most recently, they made headlines when Iranian-linked actors reportedly exploited outdated network technology to locate the phones of US personnel in the Middle East during the Iran war. But the vulnerability has been around for decades, and it’s been used for far more everyday crimes, like intercepting bank one-time passcodes. It has even been demonstrated by popular YouTubers: Veritasium hijacked a tech influencer’s calls and texts using only his phone number. This keeps happening Criminals have reportedly exploited signaling protocols in attacks on bank accounts and global telecom infrastructure. Citizen Lab exposed two long-running commercial surveillance campaigns abusing SS7 and Diameter, with thousands of attacks against targets in dozens of countries. Congressman Ted Lieu’s phone was hacked on live TV via SS7 on 60 Minutes Australia Attackers have intercepted SMS one-time passcodes to drain victims’ bank accounts. What is a signaling attack? Every call, text, and mobile data session requires your carrier to verify you’re a paying customer and route your traffic to the right destination. Carriers do this with signaling–background messages that identify your location and forward traffic accordingly. Signaling has been the connective tissue between global providers for decades, and it is one of the most overlooked attack surfaces in mobile security. Two protocols do most of the work: SS7 (from the 1970s, used in 2G/3G) and Diameter (its successor, used in 4G and most 5G). Both were designed when a small number of large operators could plug into the system, so they assume that traffic claiming to come from a legitimate operator really does. SS7 has essentially no process for authenticating the machine making a request. Diameter supports stronger authentication on paper, but operators don’t always deploy basic protections like encryption, and many fall back on the same peer-to-peer trust model. An attacker with access to the global signaling backbone, through a commercial leasing arrangement or a compromised operator, can send messages that carriers worldwide treat as trustworthy. How does it work Signaling lets an attacker ask your carrier questions and make claims on your behalf: Harvest your IMSI. Knowing your number, an attacker can request your International Mobile Subscriber ID (IMSI) under the pretense of routing a call or SMS. It can be reused for follow-on attacks for years. Locate you in real time. Queries can return the cell tower you last connected to. Others, normally reserved for emergency responders, can return the actual coordinates your phone reports. Intercept communications. The attacker claims you’ve roamed onto another network, so your calls and texts are redirected to them. Combined with a stolen username and password, this delivers your SMS second factor to the attacker instead of you. Impersonate or block you. With your IMSI, an attacker can place calls or send SMS as you. A false roaming claim can also cut off service to your phone. Disrupt networks. Deliberately misconfigured signaling messages can overwhelm provider systems. None of this touches your device. It happens in automated transactions you can’t see and that leave no trace on your phone. Why firewalls and velocity checks fall short Carrier signaling firewalls reliably block messages sent to or from the wrong place. For correctly routed messages, they often run a velocity check to test whether you could physically have traveled from your last known location to the one now claimed. If you were in New York an hour ago and a Turkish carrier says you’re on its network, the request is denied. The structural problem is that the firewall’s location data is often hours old. In research presented at the Wireless Security conference in 2025, Cape, the privacy-first mobile carrier, measured Diameter updates from a visited network arriving as infrequently as every two to ten hours. For subscribers in the US and Germany, over 250 distinct networks are reachable within a single hour of travel time. An attacker with enough operator identities will eventually find one that looks plausible. Citizen Lab’s report shows this in practice: the actor it calls STA1 repeatedly tried to track a user by rotating through eleven operator identities in nine countries to look like legitimate roaming traffic. They also pivoted between SS7 and Diameter, which most carriers defend with separate firewalls and little coordination. Consider a target who boards a flight from Nashville to Berlin and powers off her phone. A message posing as China Mobile claiming she’s roaming there gets rejected, because it’s physically impossible. A message from a carrier in nearby Nassau, Bahamas, looks plausible, and the home carrier can be fooled into routing her calls and SMS to the attacker. Protect yourself with private cell service. Most carriers track everything: where you go, who you call, what you do. Cape collects the minimum amount of information required to provide you with service, deletes call and text metadata after 24 hours, rotates your network ID to prevent tracking, defends against SIM- and network-based attacks, and more. Learn More → How Cape defends against signaling attacks Cape is a privacy-first mobile carrier, whose approach is to assume the global telecom system is compromised and build protections that keep communications private anyway. There are four layers: 1. Daily IMSI rotation. Almost every targeted signaling attack starts with an IMSI, and once an attacker has yours, it stays useful for as long as you have it. A Citizen Lab report confirms this, with the same IMSIs being attacked across operations separated by months and years. On most carriers, your IMSI is permanent. You get one when you activate your SIM and you keep it forever. On Cape, your IMSI rotates daily. The databases of harvested IMSIs that surveillance vendors build up over the years are no longer useful against Cape subscribers. 2. No SS7. Cape doesn’t support SS7 at all, and there is no SS7 fallback in the network, so SS7-based attacks have nothing to land on. Many carriers still struggle to retire legacy SS7 infrastructure because some revenue-generating part of their network depends on it. 3. Network Lock. Instead of trusting a network’s idea of where you are, Cape asks your device. When a foreign network requests to attach to your phone, Network Lock queries the Cape app, which evaluates the claim locally at the country level and reports back whether it matches. If an attacker tries to attach your IMSI from another country while your phone is at home, the request is denied and you’re notified. Cape’s systems learn only whether the claim matches, not where you actually are, and Cape never collects or stores your precise location. 4. Continuous penetration testing. Most signaling firewalls are compliance tools tuned to GSMA baseline recommendations. Those recommendations are distributed to more than 1,200 member providers, so the same guidance is available to attackers who can send signaling messages. 4wbm95.text: Suspected nation-state hackers have developed sophisticated malware designed to target a customized version of Windows used by government agencies in Asia, according to new research. The previously unknown malware, dubbed NetamLoader, uses legitimate Microsoft software components to execute malicious code, evade security tools and download additional programs onto infected computers, Russian cybersecurity firm Kaspersky said in a report Thursday. Researchers suspect the operation involved a supply-chain attack, in which hackers compromise trusted software or its distribution process to gain access to their intended targets. Kaspersky detected the malware on one computer in the first half of 2026. Its analysis suggested the attack was tailored to a specialized version of Windows 10 used exclusively by government organizations in Asia. Kaspersky did not identify the country or government agency involved, and it remains unclear how many systems may have been affected. The company said it could not link the attack to any known state-sponsored hacking group. The malware was discovered inside a package stored in a directory used for Windows operating system updates. The package contained legitimate software components, including files belonging to the third-party update management tool Patch My PC and programs digitally signed by Microsoft. Once activated, NetamLoader could interfere with Windows security scanning, conceal its activity and delete files and system logs. The malware was also capable of collecting information about infected computers, downloading additional malicious code and communicating with attacker-controlled infrastructure through encrypted connections. Researchers said the malware's ability to recognize and manipulate components of a government-specific Windows system suggested that the attackers had detailed knowledge of their intended target's technology. The attack also raised concerns about the security of customized government operating systems, researchers said. "The advantage is that each country controls the development, operation, and upgrading of its own operating systems, granting it full autonomy over the entire process. On the other hand, it also means that each country must protect this entire vast ecosystem on its own," Kaspersky said. Researchers had identified only one infected system and had not established whether the attackers had successfully stolen sensitive information. They also could not confirm how the malware reached the computer or whether the software update infrastructure itself had been compromised. u1dfjn.text: The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything. Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits. Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts. The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today. In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments. Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today. Figure 1. Operational pressures and configuration drift can delay enforcement. Build Confidence Before Enforcement Safe remediation follows four stages: Observe, Prove, Act, and Confirm. Evidence carries the proposed response through each stage, with review and approval where required. Observation starts with data your security and IT systems already produce. Vulnerability findings, IPS traffic, device utilization, endpoint policies, and configuration states show what surrounds the proposed change. Then comes proof, and the method fits the technology. An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode, giving teams evidence about false positives and performance before it progresses to Prevent. Operating system hardening can use a selected test group, with each host rechecked after execution. Endpoint settings can be assessed against the vendor's hardening baseline. The decision becomes specific to your environment. Security teams explain the protection they expect. Infrastructure and application owners judge the effect on the systems they run. Figure 2. Validation connects environmental evidence with approval, execution, and confirmation. Use Existing Controls While Waiting For a Permanent Fix Patching remains essential for addressing the underlying vulnerability. Testing, coordination, and deployment schedules can extend the time before a patch reaches production, creating a period when additional protection may be needed. An existing IPS signature or virtual patch can help block the relevant exploit path during that period. Correlating vulnerability data with control coverage shows whether a suitable protection exists and whether it is inactive, in Detect mode, or already enforced. That context helps teams select the response. A protection awaiting enforcement may be a candidate for validation and activation. An exposure without a compensating control may require urgent patching or another action. The remediation record should distinguish interim protection from a permanent fix. A compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while the underlying vulnerability remains open and requires follow through. Keep Approval and Execution Connected Once an action has been evaluated, organizations can require approval of its scope or permit automated execution through configured workflows. The approved change then runs through the system responsible for the affected control. IPS changes can use the security management server, operating system hardening can use existing patch management infrastructure, and supported endpoint changes can use the vendor API. This approach lets teams work through the technologies already deployed. Confirmation completes the process. Policy installation can establish that an IPS protection reached enforcement. Host checks can verify a hardening change. Execution records can show failed or pending actions that still need attention, alongside the user, timestamp, and associated exposure. Measure the Protection That Follows Success should include evidence that the intended protection is active after execution. Subsequent security events can show whether a newly enabled control blocked activity associated with the exposure. Across the measured organizations, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. Over one month, protections applied through remediation subsequently blocked 703.56 million attacks, including 21 million within 24 hours of remediation. These results describe the analyzed environments and provide evidence of protection following enforcement. Figure 3. Remediation outcomes across the environments measured in the white paper. Make Safe Remediation Part of Exposure Management Prioritization establishes where action should begin. Safe remediation gives teams a controlled path for carrying that decision into production, with evidence supporting the proposed change and confirmation showing its result. Check Point Exposure Management connects exposure prioritization with environmental validation, controlled execution, and confirmation through existing security technologies. Security teams can use that process to reduce exposure while evaluating the operational impact of each response. 13snl8i.text: Cryptocurrency-based prediction market Polymarket confirmed that it dealt with outages on Thursday due to a cybersecurity incident involving a third-party provider. The company suffered outages starting at 2pm EST on Thursday and eventually attributed the downtime to a compromise involving an unnamed provider. A spokesperson for the company declined to answer questions about the incident, directing Recorded Future News to a statement that said it identified and fixed an issue impacting its international platform. “One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement,” the company said. “Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online. Trading is now fully back online. We’ll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders.” The New York-based company did not say how much was stolen or by who. Several blockchain security companies traced the losses back to an account that allegedly siphoned more than $2.1 million worth of cryptocurrency from users on the site. Cybersecurity firm Hudson Rock said the unnamed third party provider was DebugBear — a company that provides website performance services. DebugBear said on Thursday that it is being “impacted by an ongoing security incident” and urged customers to remove its embed codes from their websites. According to Hudson Rock, it found evidence pointing to what it called “wallet-draining code” that was designed by someone to discover accounts, select assets and transfer funds to a designated account. Hudson Rock said it was unable to determine the number of victims or the total number of losses but did note that Polymarket removed DebugBear code from its site on Thursday. “The evidence does not identify an attacker or demonstrate a wider compromise affecting other DebugBear customers,” Hudson Rock said. Polymarket is one of the largest prediction markets in the U.S., allowing people to place bets on a variety of topics like politics, military conflicts, the weather and sports. It was banned in the U.S. until 2025, when President Donald Trump’s son joined the company as an advisor and investor. It is still banned in several countries, including France and Brazil. 1t6bjhd.text: A cyberattack forced Russian home goods retailer Poryadok to close some of its stores and suspend online services for five consecutive days, leaving customers unable to collect orders, access loyalty accounts or contact customer support. The company, which operates 48 stores across 32 Russian cities, first reported technical problems on Sunday, saying its website, mobile app and physical stores were temporarily unavailable. Poryadok later confirmed that the disruption was caused by a cyberattack but did not disclose how hackers breached its systems or when normal operations would resume. "We have been hit by a cyberattack, but we are already actively working to restore our services and gradually return operations to normal," the company said in a statement. The retailer said it expected to reopen its stores and restore access to order information and loyalty program bonuses but provided no timeline. Local media reported that stores in Voronezh, where the company was founded in 2010, and other Russian cities remained closed, with notices on their doors citing unspecified technical problems. Some customers continued to arrive at stores unaware of the closures, while others complained that they could not collect previously paid-for orders, arrange returns or reach the company's customer service hotline. In the western Russian city of Kursk, one customer reported being unable to collect an online order or extend its pickup deadline because both the company's website and physical stores were inaccessible. Customers in other cities reported similar problems. According to user reports collected by outage monitoring service DownRadar, Poryadok's online services remained unavailable on Friday. The company's website indicated that only some stores were still affected, although the full extent of the disruption remained unclear. It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack or whether any customer information had been compromised. Other Russian businesses have also reported cyberattacks on their systems over the past two months. In September, popular fast-food chain Dodo Pizza suffered a breach claimed by a hacking group calling itself DataSuckers. More recently, in mid-October, Russian online travel agency Anywayanyday temporarily suspended bookings following a cyberattack that disrupted its IT systems, preventing customers from purchasing airline and train tickets or booking hotels. 16y8qfw.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Hardware Security / Cryptocurrency A Trezor Safe 5 hardware wallet bought from the reseller CryptoBilis has an extra circuit board that sends out the recovery phrase over a mobile network, a customer has reported. Trezor has not yet examined the device. It is telling everyone who bought a Trezor from CryptoBilis since March 2026 to move their funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase. Trezor said in a blog post on October 30 that the report came in two days earlier from a customer in Indonesia. He bought the wallet from CryptoBilis in August, through the marketplace Tokopedia. The board sits between the wallet's main board and its screen, with a cellular module and an antenna, according to the report. It reads the screen, including the recovery phrase (Trezor calls it the wallet backup), and sends it out whenever the device is plugged in. Trezor has the customer's photos and description and has interviewed him on a video call. It is arranging for the wallet to be sent to its lab. Trezor finds the report believable enough to warn buyers now. "Waiting for lab confirmation would leave CryptoBilis buyers exposed in the meantime," the company said. No CryptoBilis buyer has reported losing funds to Trezor, which cannot see what customers hold in their wallets. The customer had moved his funds off the wallet before he found the board. Trezor's advice covers every Trezor model bought from CryptoBilis since March 2026, from any store that sold devices CryptoBilis supplied, including its store on Tokopedia: If you already use the wallet, move your funds to a new wallet with a new recovery phrase as soon as possible. Restoring the old recovery phrase on another device does not help, because a tampered wallet could already have sent that phrase out. If you have no other secure hardware wallet, move the funds for now to a software wallet or an exchange you know. If you have not set up the wallet, do not set it up, and never type your existing recovery phrase into it. Keep the CryptoBilis device and contact Trezor Support. Trezor will ship you a new device or give you a voucher that covers the cost of one. If you are not sure where your device came from, check the seller's name on your receipt or contact Trezor Support. As of October 30, Trezor had no reports involving any other reseller. Owners cannot reliably check a device themselves and should not weigh or open it to try it, according to Trezor. The customer noticed a weight difference, but small differences can have other causes. Trezor also expects scammers to use the incident to carry out phishing through fake emails, letters, and phone calls. Trezor dropped CryptoBilis, its authorized reseller in Southeast Asia, on October 9, after hardware wallet maker Ledger began investigating losses among Ledger customers who had bought from CryptoBilis. Ledger has since said that one affected customer's wallet contained an unauthorized hardware implant built to capture the recovery phrase during setup. Trezor says the board reported in its Safe 5 appears to work like the implants seen in Ledger devices. Trezor will not compare the two while investigations continue, because each maker builds its devices differently. It does not know who is responsible. Separate Police Advisory in Singapore The Singapore Police Force said in an advisory on October 28 that Ledger hardware wallets bought from some retail stores in Singapore contained malicious hardware components. At least two cases have been reported since September 10. The components could capture users' recovery phrases or private keys. Police investigations are ongoing, and Ledger is reviewing the affected cases.

1p9q35w.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 30, 2026Cyber Crime / Cyber Espionage Ahmad Umar Agha, a Syrian Electronic Army hacker known online as "Th3Pr0," has been sentenced by a U.S. federal court to 42 months in prison for his role in a hacking conspiracy that targeted Western news outlets. The conspiracy was organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad's inner circle, including the commander of Syria's General Intelligence Directorate, the U.S. Justice Department said on October 29. The pro-Assad Syrian Electronic Army began its attacks in 2011. Its members sent phishing emails to steal employees' passwords, then used those passwords to deface websites, redirect web traffic, and hijack social media accounts, according to a 2014 FBI affidavit. On April 23, 2013, the group hijacked the Associated Press's Twitter account and posted a false report that President Barack Obama had been injured in two explosions at the White House. Twitter's message confirming a password reset for that account was sent to a Gmail account used primarily by Agha, the affidavit says. The Justice Department said Agha carried out that hack, which caused a temporary $136 billion drop in the value of stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Agha later told Business Insider that a big drop in the Dow "was our goal of that hack attack" and that "it was a big victory for us." Agha was first charged in June 2014 in a complaint that remained secret until March 2016. That month, the FBI added him and co-defendant Firas Dardar to its Cyber's Most Wanted list with a $100,000 reward. A federal grand jury indicted both men in May 2018. Court Watch reported in December 2025 that Agha was in U.S. custody and had appeared in federal court the month before. Three earlier public documents in the case do not describe Syrian officials organizing or leading the group: the 2014 FBI affidavit, the Justice Department's March 2016 announcement of the charges, and its May 2018 announcement of the indictment. In the 2016 announcement, the department said the group acted "in support of" the Syrian government. An early study of the group, published by the OpenNet Initiative, found no credible evidence directly linking the attackers to the Syrian government beyond the unspoken support any such group would need to operate on Syrian networks. In announcing the sentence, the department also said the conspiracy collected intelligence for Assad's government, which fell in December 2024. "Agha deployed his hacking skills in the service of Assad's regime to silence reporting on the regime's atrocities, intimidate its opponents, and incite U.S. servicemembers to refuse their orders," said John A. Eisenberg, Assistant Attorney General for National Security. In all, Agha hacked about 47 Western media outlets, businesses, non-profit groups, and U.S. and allied government bodies, the department said. He got into the company that hosted the U.S. Marine Corps recruiting website and redirected its visitors to an image urging Marines to refuse their orders and fight alongside the Syrian Army. About 3,500 potential visitors saw that image instead of recruiting material. He also twice tried to take over the White House's social media accounts by stealing White House staff email passwords. Once, he got into staff email but failed to trick other staff into giving him access. The FBI affidavit describes the group breaking into a White House staff member's personal email account in July 2013 and says no official White House account was compromised. Many victims spent large sums on cleanup and security upgrades, according to court filings cited by the department. One company that supplies online publishers with content, ads, and links lost about $35,000 a day for about six months. A global non-profit group lost $480,000, including about $250,000 on new network monitoring tools, and had to retrain more than 800 staff members. Dardar remains a fugitive, the department said. He was also charged in a separate case with Peter Romar, a Syrian national then living in Germany. Romar was extradited to the U.S. and pleaded guilty in 2016.

ztq7fh.text: Microsoft has resolved Always On VPN connection failures triggered after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates. The Always On VPN remote access solution runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network when their devices connect to the Internet. It has replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. Microsoft has previously mistakenly flagged this known issue as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates. The company first acknowledged it in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying the Always On VPN failures were triggered on Windows 11 systems by the September 2026 security updates when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP. On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue has finally been fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update. "This update fixes an issue that affects Always On VPN connections after installing September security update," it said. "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed. In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'" Workaround also available Microsoft also provides a temporary fix for users who don't want to install the preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates. This requires admins to choose one of two tunneling protocols to prevent Always On VPN failures on affected devices. "IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," Microsoft said. "Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements." The October 2026 preview update also fixes a known issue preventing non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then). xaez2k.text: Drupal warned admins to patch a critical access bypass vulnerability in the Commerce Core module that attackers are exploiting in the wild. Tracked as CVE-2026-118539, this flaw stems from a missing authorization weakness that can be abused by unauthenticated attackers and affects Commerce Core versions 0.0.0 through 2.41 and 3.0.0 through 3.3.13. The Drupal security team asked admins on the 3.x branch to upgrade immediately to Commerce Core 3.3.13 (or Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 for earlier versions) and audit orders for inconsistencies, since threat actors are exploiting this vulnerability in attacks. "This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs," Drupal said in a Wednesday advisory tagged as highly critical. "The module doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor. This vulnerability is being actively exploited in the wild." Commerce Core is a community-developed Drupal module used by more than 42,000 websites, including many high-profile organizations such as Fortune 500 companies and research universities. The module provides a software framework for building and running e-commerce sites and shopping apps on top of the Drupal Content Management System (CMS). In May, Drupal also warned that attackers were exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could lead to privilege escalation, information disclosure, and remote code execution. Days later, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered federal agencies to patch their systems within three days. Two weeks ago, Drupal patched two more remote code execution security issues (CVE-2026-108097 and CVE-2026-108099) that could allow threat actors to execute code remotely, and urged admins to apply updates as soon as possible because attackers could develop exploits "within hours or days." Over the last several years, CISA has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, two of which have also been abused by ransomware gangs. 34wxbk.text: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has linked the theft of about $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency to a DevOps engineer's compromised laptop. The crypto exchange said the access let attackers submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions after they accessed a service container, and it hasn't yet found evidence of a leaked wallet private key. "To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer's permissions, and this was not a single 'one-click' action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual," Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said. Binance also said it "uncovered additional points of breach" but was "still gathering the facts, and will share more directly as we have them." The company confirmed the breach in a statement shared with BleepingComputer on Thursday and reassured customers that their funds were safe. "Binance will cover all losses from the SAFU fund and the company's funds. User funds are safe. We will also publish an updated Proof of Reserves once the remediation is complete," it said. Since the attack, Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it conducts security checks, revoked authorizations for the affected address, and is working with blockchain intelligence partners and law enforcement to trace and recover the stolen funds. Crypto theft linked to North Korean hackers Although the company didn't link the incident to a hacking group or threat actor, blockchain analysis firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking unit also tracked as Lazarus Group and APT38. "On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the USD 1.5 billion Bybit hack of February 2025," TRM said. Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis confirmed TRM Labs' findings, stating with "a high degree of confidence" that TraderTraitor is responsible for the Binance $6.4 billion hack. While stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, Ripple, and others have frozen roughly $2.7 billion since the incident, the attackers still have control of about $2.4 billion that can't be frozen. "Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about USD 2.67 billion in stablecoins, and Arbitrum's Security Council froze 8,426 ETH and 74.6 million ARB on its network, for a total of roughly USD 2.7 billion," TRM added. "The attacker raced the freezes by selling USDT to market makers and borrowing ETH against USDT on Aave. It now holds more than 420,000 ETH and 18,270 BTC, about USD 2.4 billion in assets beyond any issuer's reach." The TraderTraitor hackers were previously linked to many other major crypto theft incidents, including the theft of $1.5 billion in the February 2025 Bybit hack. At $6.36 billion, the Binance attack is now the largest recorded crypto heist. 1jq8q8n.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 30, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Drupal has warned that threat actors are exploiting a "highly critical" security flaw in its Commerce Core component. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-118539 (CVSS score: N/A), is a case of missing authorization affecting Commerce Core versions from 0.0.0 to 2.41 and from 3.0.0 to 3.3.13. "This module enables you to sell goods and services to customers through an included shopping cart and checkout form or through decoupled applications via APIs," Drupal said in an advisory. "The module doesn't sufficiently protect certain routes and entity fields, leading to an access bypass that may financially impact the vendor." The open-source content-management framework acknowledged that the vulnerability is being "actively exploited in the wild," but provided no specifics about the nature of the activity or the extent of the campaign. Users are being recommended to update to the latest version - Version 3.x - Upgrade to Commerce Core 3.3.13 Earlier versions - Upgrade to Commerce Core 8.x-2.41 Drupal has credited researchers Dan Puccetti (dpuccetti), Marcus Johansson (marcus_johansson), and Robert Snyder (rsnyd) with reporting the flaw. The development comes as two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), and collectively referred to as PHP2Shell, are witnessing active exploitation attempts in the wild. As of October 25, the percentage of organizations significantly affected by PHP2Shell has declined to 52.1%, according to data from Google-owned Wiz. The cloud security company said it has so far observed two types of activities, including attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism that match public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. The other category refers to "PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application," Wiz researchers Yaara Shriki, Shahar Dorfman, Alma Blachsan, and Yaron Samuel said. "Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own."

1ndcl3g.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed that a trojanized version of Anthropic's official Claude Code extension was distributed through the Cursor Marketplace as a legitimate update, attempting to install a persistent SSH backdoor on affected systems. The malicious update, version 2.1.313, was distributed under the extension's legitimate publisher identity, prompting Cursor to temporarily shut down its marketplace to remove the compromised package. The exact method attackers used to introduce the unauthorized update remains unclear. "We identified a security incident affecting a modified Claude Code VS Code extension accessed through our Cursor IDE extension marketplace, impacting at most 5,000 users," Cursor said. "This malicious version of the extension was not developed by Anthropic. It does not impact other extensions downloaded from the cursor[.]com/marketplace, Grok Bot, Grok, or our other SpaceXSI product. However, Cursor's statement that the malicious version "was not developed by Anthropic" misses the point. The attackers distributed it as version 2.1.313 under Anthropic's legitimate Claude Code extension ID (anthropic.claude-code), rather than as a separate fake extension. "The package identifies itself as anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313, but its main JavaScript bundle contains a malicious 66-line loader inserted before the legitimate extension code," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. The malicious update was distributed only through Cursor's marketplace, with no evidence that it reached Open VSX or Microsoft's official VS Code Marketplace. Users who installed Claude Code through either of those marketplaces are not known to be affected by this incident. As of October 30, 2026, the malicious version has been removed, and Anthropic has published version 2.1.314 to both Open VSX and Microsoft VS Code Marketplace. The extension is designed to activate after VS Code startup and when its webview opens, then proceeds to add an attacker-controlled key to the user's "~/.ssh/authorized_keys" file. The key is labeled "svc-telemetry" in an attempt to make it appear harmless. Subsequently, it attempts to make the victim reachable through SSH across Windows, Linux, and macOS, establishes a reverse tunnel to "134.209.82[.]225," installs platform-specific persistence in the form of a scheduled task, crontab, and LaunchAgent, and transmits host reconnaissance data to "134.209.82[.]225:8099/beacon" on port 8099 over an unencrypted HTTP request. "Turning on the local SSH service requires admin rights, which the malicious extension does not have on most macOS and Windows hosts," the SpaceXAI-owned company said in its own analysis of the incident. "On those hosts the step fails and the attacker could not have logged in through the tunnel. The extension still adds the attacker's SSH key, installs persistence, and sends host details to the attacker. Follow the remediation steps below regardless." The collected data includes - Public IP address from api.ipify[.]org Hostname and local username Operating system and CPU architecture Home directory and current working directory Global Git email from git config --global user.email Names of up to 40 environment variables containing KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP "Environment-variable values are not placed directly in the initial beacon," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "Their names can still reveal which cloud providers, CI systems, and credential types are configured. More importantly, successful SSH access would allow the operator to inspect the account directly." No other follow-on payloads have been observed. That said, the establishment of a reverse tunnel provides a pathway to the victim's SSH service, allowing the operator to issue commands or transfer files. "It was pulled very quickly, but anyone who has their Claude Code instance set to auto-update could have consumed the malware," Gile said. Cursor has revealed that the incident has affected at most 5,000 users who installed the malicious version between about 2:27 a.m. and 1:35 p.m. PT on October 29, 2026. The company also said that it will be reaching out to impacted users directly. Users who have installed the compromised extension during the window are advised to isolate the hosts, remove the unauthorized SSH key and persistence mechanisms, and rotate credentials and sessions. The disclosure comes a little over a week after an unknown attacker replaced the release binaries of five already-published versions of OVHcloud's official CLI ("ovh/ovhcloud-cli") with a secret-stealing malware after uploading them through a GitHub account of a legitimate OVH contributor ("HassenBF") hijacked in March 2026 as part of the GlassWorm operation. (An earlier version of the story stated that the extension on the Open VSX registry was compromised. The incident has since been traced back to a compromise of the Cursor VS Code Marketplace.)
